Notably, these changes occured without detectable loss of epithelial tissue integrity. Together, our findings identify epithelial polarity disruption as a mechanism through which extracellular P. aeruginosa remodels the host cytoskeleton and alters tissue mechanics during infection.

Title: Metabolic stress reveals widespread accumulation of cap-unmethylated RNAs
Authors: Xing, Z.; Sutter, B. M.; Freitas, A. V.; Dang, N. K.; Ingolia, N. T.; Tu, B. P.
Abstract: RNA polymerase II transcripts are capped with N7-methylguanosine (mG), a conserved modification important for mRNA function. Although traditionally viewed as constitutive, we developed a mass spectrometry-based method to demonstrate that in both yeast and mammalian cells, a substantial population of mRNAs lack cap methylation in response to SAM-limiting conditions and other stress conditions, which may be frequently encountered across organisms. Through developing two transcriptome-wide approaches, we found that methylation is enriched on specific transcripts and uncovered an unexpected connection between histone H3K36me3 and cap methylation, with both marks preferentially associated with stress-responsive MAPK signaling pathways. Strikingly, cap-unmethylated mRNAs exhibit features of canonical mRNAs. They are polyadenylated, exported to the cytosol, and translated. Enforced cap methylation reduces cell growth under SAM limitation, suggesting that unmethylated mRNAs confer an adaptive advantage during stress. These findings establish mRNA cap methylation as a modification responsive to metabolic stress and a previously underappreciated layer of gene expression control.

Title: AlphaGenome Enhances Personal Gene Expression Prediction but Retains Key Limitations
Authors: Kashyap, S.; Ramakrishnan, A.; Shen, L.
Abstract: Recent years have seen rapid growth in sequence-to-function (S2F) models that predict diverse molecular readouts from DNA sequence alone. However, these models have faced criticism for their limited accuracy in predicting individual-level gene expression. AlphaGenome, a state-of-the-art S2F model, excels across a range of sequence-based prediction tasks, but its utility for personal expression prediction remains incompletely assessed. Here, we evaluate AlphaGenome's ability to predict tissue-specific, personal gene expression and find that it significantly outperforms its predecessor, Enformer. Across 1,000 genes and 11,471 eligible gene-tissue pairs, AlphaGenome significantly outperforms Enformer for 3,103 pairs, whereas Enformer significantly outperforms AlphaGenome for 828 pairs, yielding a win ratio of 3.75. This imbalance is supported by a global permutation test (P = 2.0e-4), with a median correlation difference of 0.046. Nevertheless, pretrained AlphaGenome substantially underperforms Elastic Net and Random Forest trained on individual-level data. These findings demonstrate that AlphaGenome better captures individual-specific gene expression variation than Enformer, while highlighting substantial room for improvement in sequence-based prediction of personal gene expression.

Title: A high-resolution protein-RNA binding atlas for structure-aware interaction prediction and post-transcriptional regulatory modeling
Authors: Karimzadeh, M.; Fish, L.; Karner, H.; Linder, J.; Emadi, A.; Hernandez-Corchado, A.; Smaili, F. Z.; Stewart, E. M.; Kelley, D. R.; Wang, B.; Najafabadi, H. S.; Leonetti, M.; Goodarzi, H.
Abstract: RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) control post-transcriptional gene expression by regulating RNA processing, localization, stability, and translation. However, our understanding of RNA regulation remains limited by the resolution, scale, and uniformity of available RBP binding maps. Here we introduce eclair CLIP (ecCLIP), a high-throughput CLIP-seq platform that combines endogenous protein tagging for uniform affinity capture with ligation-free library preparation to generate high-resolution RNA-protein binding profiles. We applied ecCLIP to 67 endogenously tagged RBPs in HEK293T cells, generating a high-quality transcriptome-scale atlas that recovered known binding preferences and captured post-transcriptional regulons linked to RNA half-life. To test the utility of the atlas, we incorporated ecCLIP into Borzuki, a Borzoi-derived sequence-to-function model trained on complementary RNA degradation, expression, CLIP, and Perturb-seq data. Inclusion of ecCLIP data improved RNA half-life prediction and assessment of 3' UTR variant effects on RNA stability, demonstrating that our atlas helps capture RNA dynamics. To directly model the cis-regulatory grammar underlying these RBP-RNA interactions, we developed Pythia, a structure-aware neural network architecture that incorporates context-free grammar-inspired fixed convolutions to explicitly encode RNA base-pairing features. Pythia predicted RBP binding from sequence and structural context and decomposed predictions into sequence- and structure-dependent components. We tested this decomposition for five RBPs using massively parallel reporter CLIP (MPRC) binding assays in cells, using synthetic RNA libraries containing mutations designed to preserve or disrupt predicted RNA structures across nominated binding sites. We used the same MPRC strategy to confirm allele-specific binding effects for variants prioritized by Pythia. Together, ecCLIP and Pythia provide a resource for structure-aware decoding of RNA-protein interaction grammar and interpretation of post-transcriptional regulatory variation.

Title: Shared genomic signatures of Arctic adaptation among distantly related plant lineages
Authors: Elphinstone, C.; Sandler, M.; Stone, P.; Torres Jimenez, M. F.; Henn, J. J.; Zhang, X.; Birkeland, S.; Brochmann, C.; Henry, G. H. R.; Todesco, M.; Bacon, C. D.; Rieseberg, L. H.
Abstract: Extreme environments impose strong selection pressures that can drive convergent adaptation among distantly related species. Arctic plants survive low temperatures, 24-hour light in summer and darkness in winter, short growing seasons, limited precipitation, nutrient-poor soils, and extreme seasonal variation. To test if these conditions are associated with shared genomic signatures, we generated a chromosome-level genome assembly for Oxyria digyna and compared it with existing reference genomes for three distantly related Arctic species (Cochlearia groenlandica, Draba nivalis, Dryas octopetala) and for 16 non-Arctic species from the same families. We identified 214 orthogroups with signatures of positive selection in all Arctic species, 1.6 times the number shared among the non-Arctic species. Although no gene ontology (GO) categories remained significantly enriched after multiple-testing correction, descriptive annotations included genes involved in general functions including protein folding, glycolysis, transcription, and oxidative-stress responses. Orthogroups showing copy number variation were associated with biotic interactions, sexual reproduction, and nutrient acquisition, suggesting that species may respond to biotic and nutrient stresses by shifts in gene copy number. Arctic and alpine genomes contained lower proportions of some repetitive elements, including terminal inverted repeats, and smaller regions of centromeric repeats than non-Arctic genomes. Overall, we see shared genes under positive selection, similar functions of genes with high copy number variation, and lower counts of some repetitive elements in the Arctic plant genomes. Our findings reveal a shared genomic signature of Arctic adaptation across deeply diverged plant lineages, suggesting that evolution in extreme environments repeatedly targets similar genomic features.

Title: Identification and inhibition of the Cyclin D Rb-docking interface that drives cell division
Authors: Topacio, B. R.; Fleming, C.; Lanz, M.; Ord, M.; Memarpoor-Yazdi, M.; Zhang, S.; Xie, S.; Tuvikene, J.; Weaver, A.; Sanidas, I.; Davey, N.; Pryciak, P.; Sage, J.; Rubin, S.; Koivomagi, M.; Skotheim, J.
Abstract: The animal cell division cycle is initiated by the cyclin-dependent kinases CDK4 and CDK6 in complex with D-type cyclins. Cyclin D-CDK4/6 complex formation is promoted by the assembly factors p21 and p27, which bind both subunits. p27 binds the hydrophobic patch on cyclin D that is similar to the patch used by other cell cycle cyclins to dock their substrates. This raised the question as to how cyclin D could find its substrates if its hydrophobic patch were already occupied? Here, we show that D-type cyclins use their A2' helix to dock the retinoblastoma protein Rb, a key substrate regulating cell cycle progression. The specific interface of cyclin D's A2' helix is unique among cyclins and its mutation slows proliferation. Taken together, our work identifies a cyclin D-substrate docking mechanism that can be targeted by novel cancer therapeutics.

Title: A High-Sensitivity and High-Throughput LC-MS Workflow for Low-Input and Single-Cell Proteomics
Authors: Okuda, Y.; Watanabe, S.; Endo, Y.; Konno, R.; Mitsui, H.; Nakajima, D.; Kodera, Y.; Ohara, O.; Higo, D.; Kawashima, Y.
Abstract: Single-cell proteomics (SCP) requires sample preparation that minimizes sample loss and highly sensitive LC-MS analysis because the amount of protein available from a single cell is extremely limited. Here, we developed an integrated workflow for low-input and single-cell proteomics based on single-cell proteomics by LMNG-assisted sample preparation (scpLASP), which enables microliter-scale sample preparation using standard laboratory consumables. Systematic optimization of peptide reconstitution conditions identified 0.01% n-dodecyl-{beta}-D-maltoside (DDM) combined with 0.01% lauryl maltose neopentyl glycol (LMNG) as the condition yielding the highest number of identified peptides among those tested for low-input samples. Optimization of the LC mobile-phase composition identified 0.5% acetic acid with 1% dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) as the optimal condition, increasing the mean number of identified protein groups from 6,767 with 0.1% formic acid to 7,409 for 250 pg HeLa digests analyzed using an Orbitrap Astral Zoom. Shortening the LC gradient from 11 to 5.5 min enabled higher analytical throughput while maintaining mean identification counts of 6,558 and 7,088 protein groups from 100 and 250 pg HeLa digests, respectively, with median protein-level coefficients of variation of 9.20% and 6.99%. When the optimized workflow was applied to HEK293-derived Expi293F single cells using the same 5.5-min LC gradient, an effective analytical throughput of 135 samples per day was achieved with an injection volume of 4.5 {micro}L, accounting for sample-loading time. This workflow identified a median of 5,655 protein groups per cell using an empirical spectral library generated from 20-cell samples. Overall, this study establishes a sensitive and high-throughput workflow for low-input and single-cell proteomics that combines low-loss microliter-scale sample preparation with optimized LC-MS analysis, achieving high proteome depth and analytical throughput without requiring specialized nanoliter-scale sample-preparation devices.

Title: Scooby-2: fine-tuning AlphaGenome for single-cell genomic track prediction
Authors: Hingerl, J. C.; Gagneur, J.
Abstract: Sequence-to-function models predict genomic tracks from DNA sequence. AlphaGenome has been shown to outperform previous models, including Borzoi, on most track-prediction and variant-effect benchmarks. However, like its predecessors, it predicts tracks only for predefined, mostly bulk-derived cell types and tissues. While Scooby has extended Borzoi to single-cell resolution, a single-cell adaptation of AlphaGenome is still lacking. We present Scooby-2, which combines AlphaGenome with a cell-specific decoder to predict single-cell RNA-seq coverage and chromatin-accessibility genomic tracks from DNA sequence. The package provides the implementation, the parameter-efficient fine-tuning setup, the training pipeline and inference scripts. When evaluated on the NeurIPS bone marrow single-cell dataset, Scooby-2 achieved a Pearson correlation of 0.56 when predicting cell-type-specific gene expression differences, compared with 0.53 for Scooby. When using the distilled AlphaGenome backbone, variant effect prediction concordance of fine-mapped eQTLs from the OneK1K cohort improved from 0.37 to 0.47 Spearman's rank correlation across all associations, an improvement consistent with that of AlphaGenome over Borzoi itself.

Title: Joint localization and testing reveals spatial context of differential expression
Authors: Stotzem, N.; Chang, S.; Cai, N.; Casale, F. P.
Abstract: Multi-subject spatial transcriptomics is increasingly used to identify molecular differences across individuals and conditions while resolving where in tissue those differences occur. Yet subject-level differential expression (DE) analyses commonly require spatial regions to be specified in advance, separating localization from testing. Here we present SpaceDX, a framework that uses gene-specific attention-based spatial weighting to jointly test differential expression and localize the spatial expression patterns contributing to these associations. In simulations, SpaceDX outperforms cluster-based DE methods when differential expression does not align with predefined spatial boundaries. Across two multi-subject mouse brain datasets, SpaceDX detected 45.8% more DE genes than regional DESeq2 pseudobulk in a chronic stress model, while in an Alzheimer's disease model combining SpaceDX with DESeq2 increased discovery by 19.1% relative to DESeq2 alone. Across both datasets, the learned maps provided spatial context for condition-associated expression signals in addition to gene-level significance. In the chronic stress model, for example, oligodendrocyte- and myelin-associated genes showed shared localization to corresponding brain structures. Together, these results show that the spatial context of differential expression can be inferred jointly with gene-level associations, recovering signals obscured by regional aggregation without requiring the relevant tissue context to be defined in advance.

Title: MutQA: A Cross-Validated Q&A Dataset for Genetic Mutations
Authors: McCourt, R.; Arredondo, D.; Macaulay, O.; Poshiya, S.; Edeh, O.; Virupakshappa, K.; Nguyen Bach, M.; Almeida Ruiz, E.; Hu, Y.; Tafoya, L. E.; Hudgens, D. P.; Kundnani, D.; Sahu, A.
Abstract: We introduce MutQA, a dataset of 330,387 citation-grounded question-answer (QA) pairs linking genetic mutations to their functional consequences as described in the biomedical literature. Each record pairs a protein-coding mutation with a natural-language question and an evidence-backed answer anchored to sentences in one of 27,442 open-access PubMed Central articles, spanning 6,620 genes and 125,593 gene-variant pairs. The dataset is constructed using CrossValQA, a framework that enforces information isolation between independent LLMs: one model generates QA pairs from an article, a second model answers the same question without access to the first model's response, and a third model judges whether each model's rationale supports the other's answer, so that retained QA pairs are reproducible from the source text rather than hallucinated. Of 401,406 audited QA pairs, 82.7% pass both directions of this cross-validation; those with a recoverable reference protein sequence form the released benchmark. In a 999-pair stratified audit, two expert annotators agree exactly on 86.4% of cross-validated QA pairs (95% CI 83.7-89.0; n = 638), a tier in which about 90% of ratings are "correct". Individual LLM judges agree with individual annotators at a comparable 87.0% on this tier but far less on QA pairs that fail cross-validation. Fine-tuning MutaPLM on MutQA nearly doubles its mean LLM-judge score for question-conditioned mutation-effect answering (1.45 to 2.82 on a 0-5 scale) and improves mutation-recovery accuracy from effect descriptions from 19.4% to 32.1%. Providing variant-matched MutQA retrieval context, without fine-tuning, improves strict answer accuracy across four LLM families by 20.0-28.6 percentage points, demonstrating the framework's ability to improve the reliability of LLM answers. We also apply CrossValQA to proteomics, providing a proof of concept for its use beyond mutation-specific QA. We release the dataset, construction framework, and evaluation code.

Title: WITHDRAWN: PD-L2 Regulates Natural Antibody and IL-10 Secretion by B-1 cells
Authors: Amendt, T.; Vanes, L.; Tybulewicz, V.
Abstract: The authors have withdrawn this manuscript because of concerns regarding the reliability of the data. Therefore, the authors do not wish this work to be cited as reference for the project. If you have any questions, please contact the corresponding author.

Title: Efficient biological design via genomic in-context learning
Authors: Brixi, G.; Hao, Y. A.; Nori, D.; Merchant, A.; Widatalla, T.; King, S.; Shalvarjian, K.; Park, D.; Hie, B.
Abstract: In-context learning (ICL), the ability to perform new tasks from a few examples supplied in a prompt, is a defining emergent capability of large language models. Here, we show that ICL emerges in the genome language model Evo 2 and enables biological design. With as few as four examples in the prompt and no additional training, Evo 2 generates realistic metal-binding proteins, de novo antibodies, protein-RNA systems, and entire bacteriophage genomes. For {Phi}X174-like bacteriophage design, ICL surpasses previously fine-tuned models on computational measures of design quality and diversity. Beyond {Phi}X174, conditioning the model with different phage prompts enables us to efficiently design MS2 and M13 genomes in silico without fine-tuning. Iteratively updating the prompt with newly generated phage genomes, which we refer to as genomic chain-of-thought, further improves the diversity of designs while maintaining quality metrics. Paired with an inference engine that accelerates generation up to 35-fold and extends practicable context to a megabase, these results establish ICL as a versatile and efficient paradigm for biological sequence design.

Title: A Synthetic Virology Platform for Rapid Prototyping of Influenza A Virus mutants
Authors: Murti, J. R.; Schön, K.; Angeletti, D.
Abstract: Influenza A virus (IAV) remains a significant public health threat, with the need for effective vaccines and antiviral therapies remaining a high priority. In vitro testing is paramount in studying novel IAV viruses and their immunogenicity. To address this need, we developed a synthetic virology approach to rapidly prototype and test IAV mutants with altered antigenic sites. By strategically inserting restriction sites within an ambisense plasmid, we generated a tool where we can seamlessly replace either 1) the full hemagglutinin (HA), 2) the HA globular head domain to generate head/stalk chimeras or 3) the five canonical antigenic sites. The cloning inserts can be computationally designed and artificially synthesized, enabling rescue of synthetic Influenza A viruses. Using this platform we rescued IAV H1N1, H3N2 & H5N1, and went on to prototype their respective antigenic site mutants & chimeric IAVs using viral genome sequence alone. This platform could be useful for generating vaccine seed strains or to study anti-viral immunity.

Title: Refactored intracellular domains enhance CAR expression and function
Authors: Bai, L.; Kumar, A.; Desai, H. J.; Li, J.; de Alwis, D. P.; Hazuda, D.; Grigoryan, G.; Wang, W.; Yi, J.
Abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) intracellular domains (ICDs) couple antigen recognition to T-cell activation. Here we worked with AI agents to refactor CAR ICDs, proposing designs and refining them as measurements accumulated over three rounds. This approach yielded KRGR-{zeta}1-40, a 45-amino-acid ICD less than a third the length of the clinical 4-1BB-CD3{zeta} (BB{zeta}) ICD. Compared with BB{zeta}, KRGR-{zeta}1-40 increased CAR surface expression and antigen-driven IFN-{gamma} release, without detectable antigen-independent IFN-{gamma} release. KRGR-{zeta}1-40 extended CAR expression and target-cell killing after transient mRNA delivery, supported the expression of four CARs from a shared mRNA dose, and enhanced B-cell depletion after lentiviral and lipid-nanoparticle delivery. These results show that iterative agent-guided design with experimental feedback can yield compact ICDs that enhance CAR expression and sustain CAR T-cell function.

Title: Interpreting Graph Neural Networks for Antibacterial Drug Repurposing against Acinetobacter baumannii
Authors: Romano, S.; Grassia, M.; Righelli, D.; Lio, P.; Mangioni, G.; Taccioli, C.
Abstract: Antimicrobial resistance in Acinetobacter baumannii, whose carbapenem-resistant strains are classified by the World Health Organization as a critical priority, has motivated machine-learning screens for new antibacterials, but translating predictions into chemical hypotheses requires evaluating the molecular features on which a model relies. A graph neural network ensemble achieves competitive predictive performance against a descriptor-augmented reference model on the same antibacterial screen while using only atom features and connectivity, allowing interpretation to focus on the molecular graph without a separate input of handcrafted descriptors. The atom-level explanations identify features supporting the model's activity predictions under perturbation and restoration, while comparisons with equally sized perturbations within each molecule distinguish piperazine as the most consistently supported recurring contributor to predicted activity. Prospective screening of the Drug Repurposing Hub followed by developability and safety assessment yields a ranked shortlist for experimental follow-up and leads to testing of CE3F4, which reduced A. baumannii growth by 57% at 0.25 mM in a preliminary assay with a non-monotonic concentration--response profile.

Title: A Synthetic Consensus Chiroptera IFN-β Induces IFN-I Signaling Across Diverse Bat Taxa
Authors: Bullock, J. R.; Bulloch, B.; McBain, A.; Hill, T.; Carmody, A. B.; He, Y.; De Sousa Paula, L.; Beare, P. A.; Martens, C.; Wickenhagen, A.; van Tol, S.
Abstract: Bat-associated viruses consistently spill over from bats into humans and other animals. Many bat-associated viruses, including Marburg virus and Nipah virus, cause severe disease in humans but their presentation is subclinical in bats. Advancements in tools and resources to study bat innate antiviral immune responses, including the type I IFN (IFN-I) pathway, are needed to evaluate the mechanisms that underlie differential infection outcomes between reservoir bats and spillover hosts. Commercially available IFN-Is are not bat-specific, and conspecific IFN-Is are impractical to produce for the over 1,500 described bat species. Here, we design and validate a bat order-level consensus IFN (Chiroptera IFN-{beta}) that is functional in bat cells from six diverse bat families, including representatives from both suborders. Using Jamaican fruit bat cells, we demonstrate that Chiroptera IFN-{beta} induces an IFN-stimulated gene repertoire comparable to conspecific IFN-{beta}. This valuable resource can accelerate the capacity of the field to study bat innate antiviral responses and illuminate differences between bats and humans.

Title: Limited cross strain CMV protection by a bivalent (gB/pp65) vaccine is based on an impaired gB antibody response and evasion of pp65 cell mediated immunity
Authors: Choi, K. Y.; Qin, Y.; El-Hamdi, N.; McGregor, A.
Abstract: Congenital CMV (cCMV) is a leading cause of hearing loss and cognitive impairment in newborns and a vaccine is a high priority. The guinea pig with species-specific guinea pig cytomegalovirus (GPCMV) is the only small animal model for cCMV. Prior GPCMV vaccine studies have focused on prototype strain 22122 and not evaluated cross-strain protection, an important vaccine benchmark. The essential viral entry gB glycoprotein is an immunodominant antibody target and considered a corner stone of a CMV vaccine. Trimeric gB antigen induces potent neutralizing antibody titers but a clinical strain of GPCMV (TAMYC) is highly cell-associated limiting gB antibody cross-strain protection. In HCMV and GPCMV tegument protein pp65 is a major T cell antigen and important for convalescent immunity. A defective adenovirus (Ad) vaccine strategy encoding GPCMV gB and pp65 (AdgB+AdGP83) was evaluated for cross-strain protection. Vaccinated animals induced a cell-mediated response via IFN{gamma} ELISPOT assay against pp65 peptides conserved between strains. Additionally, the combined vaccine produced similar anti-gB and prefusion gB titers to historical sera from a standalone trimeric gB vaccine (AdgB). However, antibody response to gB(AD-1) oligomerization domain was impaired in the combined vaccine compared to historical AdgB vaccine sera which resulted in reduced neutralizing titer that were more similar to naturally convalescent GPCMV infected animals. In a pathogenicity study, vaccinated animals had partial protection against clinical TAMYC GPCMV strain challenge (SQ) compared to non-vaccinated control group. However, the vaccine failed to prevent viremia or virus dissemination to target organs, including the salivary glands, a notable limitation. Potentially, TAMYC virus evades T cell response against pp65 by dramatically reducing levels of pp65 expression compared to prototype 22122 strain. Overall, results indicate that a combination vaccine offers limited cross-strain protection despite prior success of separate pp65 or gB vaccines against GPCMV (22122 strain) and conservation of antigens between strains.

Title: Extensive and heterogeneous viral circular RNA production during Zika virus infection
Authors: Stradiotto, M.; Vezzi, A.; Vardeu, M.; Mercorelli, B.; Vogiatzis, S.; Loregian, A.; Barzon, L.; Toppo, S.; Lavezzo, E.; Trevisan, M.
Abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are covalently closed RNA molecules with regulatory functions. Although virus-derived circRNAs (vcircRNAs) are well characterized in DNA viruses, their occurrence in RNA viruses remains poorly understood. Recent reports in coronaviruses and hepatitis C virus suggest that vcircRNA production extends beyond nuclear-replicating viruses. Here, we show that Zika virus (ZIKV), a vector-borne orthoflavivirus, produces vcircRNAs during infection of neural stem cells. Using a custom computational pipeline optimized for viral back-splice junction detection, we identified at 72 hours post infection a core set of 113 putative vcircRNAs shared across three biological replicates and distributed throughout the viral genome. Eight candidates spanning different genomic regions and abundance levels were experimentally validated by rolling-circle reverse transcription and Nanopore sequencing. These findings provide the first evidence of vcircRNA production in an orthoflavivirus, suggesting that circular RNA biogenesis may represent a previously underappreciated feature of RNA virus biology.

Title: Automated anaerobic cultivation and phenotyping of diverse chain-elongating bacteria
Authors: Howard, J. P.; Lawson, C. E.
Abstract: Anaerobic bacteria perform diverse metabolic functions with considerable biotechnological potential, yet their physiology remains poorly characterized because conventional anaerobic cultivation is low throughput. Here, we developed a Platform for Automated Cultivation of Microbial Anaerobes (PACMAN) and applied it to systematically characterize the physiology of diverse chain-elongating bacteria (CEB) that produce medium-chain carboxylic acids (MCCAs). High-throughput screening across nine CEB and 20 potential electron donors revealed extensive metabolic diversity, including previously unreported conversion of glycerol to octanoate by Pseudoramibacter alactolyticus and xylose to hexanoate by Caproiciproducens sp. 7D4C2. Comparison with genome-derived metabolic pathways further revealed widespread discrepancies between predicted and observed substrate utilization. Across diverse CEB and electron donors, decreasing the acetate-to-electron-donor ratio consistently shifted product distributions toward longer-chain carboxylates, revealing a general principle governing chain-length specificity, although maximum attainable chain length remained strain dependent. Finally, screening CEB across increasing carboxylate concentrations revealed substantial variation in MCCA tolerance, with Gram-positive MCCA producers exhibiting greater resilience than Gram-negative and butyrate-producing bacteria. Together, these findings reveal organizing principles underlying the metabolic versatility and product specificity of CEB and establish automated anaerobic phenotyping as a scalable approach for discovering microbial functions relevant to biomanufacturing.

Title: AP2-L-Dependent Processes Promote PVM Maintenance and Plasmodium Liver-stage Development
Authors: Kidane, D. T.; Thaniana, A.; Mosaddeque, F.; Louvat, C.; Subudhi, A. K.; Pain, A.; Bhanot, P.
Abstract: Successful malaria infection requires transformation of Plasmodium sporozoites into replicative exo-erythrocytic forms (EEFs) within hepatocytes, a process requiring a functional parasitophorous vacuole membrane (PVM) and interactions with host cellular pathways. ApiAP2 transcription factors regulate developmental progression throughout the Plasmodium life cycle. AP2-L consists of an extended amino terminal region and two AP2 domains and is highly expressed in asexual stage trophozoites, sporozoites and early EEFs, but its role in these stages is poorly understood. We characterized the functional consequences of deleting the entire P. berghei ap2-l coding sequence on the erythrocytic cycle in vivo, sporozoite gene expression, liver-stage development, and hepatocyte-parasite interactions. AP2L-KO parasites maintained erythrocytic replication but sporozoite inoculation failed to establish blood-stage infection in mice. AP2-L loss decreased transcripts encoding proteins involved in sporozoite gliding motility, host-cell entry, and rhoptry secretion. Motif discovery upstream of a subset of these genes suggests possible direct targets of AP2-L. Infected HepG2 cells showed reduced EEF numbers and sizes, impaired parasite DNA replication, and abnormal parasite positioning relative to the host nucleus. PVMs of AP2L-KO parasites exhibited aberrant localization of proteins, absence of tubular vacuolar network extensions, and sensitivity to detergent. These abnormalities were accompanied by increased accumulation of the host's autophagy-associated protein around parasites, suggesting efficient host-mediated elimination. Additionally, AP2L-KO parasites displayed reduced association with the host microtubule-organizing center, Golgi compartments, and COPB2-positive vesicular structures, suggesting an impairment in uptake of nutrients. Together, these findings demonstrate that AP2-L directs both vacuolar biogenesis and host cytoskeletal/vesicular capture in liver-stage parasites.

Title: Kinetochore Proteins CENPB and LIC2 are critical for Episome Persistence and Replication of Kaposis's Sarcoma-Associated Herpesvirus
Authors: Singh, R. K.; Zhang, S.; Bose, D.; Ma, N.; Vangala, R.; Chunduru, K.; Robertson, E. S.
Abstract: Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) establishes lifelong latency by maintaining its genome as circular episomes tethered to host chromatin and faithfully segregated during mitosis. This process is primarily mediated by the latency-associated nuclear antigen (LANA), which interacts with host chromosome-associated factors to ensure viral genome persistence. Several kinetochore proteins, including CENP-F, Bub1, BubR1, Aurora B, Survivin, and NuMA, have been implicated in this process, yet the broader contribution of kinetochore components remains poorly defined. We performed a systematic shRNA-based screen of the 37 host genes encoding kinetochore-associated proteins to evaluate their role in KSHV episome maintenance. We validated involvement of previously reported factors and identified Centromere Protein B (CENP-B) and Light Intermediate Chain 2 of the dynein complex (LIC2) as novel kinetochore-associated proteins critical for KSHV episome persistence. Loss of these proteins significantly reduced episome stability, highlighting previously unrecognized host-virus interactions at the chromosome segregation machinery. These findings identify critical host factors that expand the repertoire of kinetochore proteins co-opted by KSHV for episome maintenance and provide new mechanistic insights into how viral episomes exploit host chromosome segregation pathways for long-term persistence. Our work underscores kinetochore proteins as a broader class of host dependency factors in gamma-herpesvirus biology and suggests potential therapeutic targets for KSHV-associated malignancies.

Title: Viral diversity and activity in Arctic tundra soils in wintertime
Authors: Juvonen, W.; Forgia, M.; Viitamäki, S.; Hultman, J.; Demina, T.
Abstract: Arctic soils store vast amounts of carbon and are warming faster than the rest of the globe. Still, little is known about microbe-mediated feedback responses to the ongoing environmental changes in the warming Arctic. Specifically, viral diversity, functions, and virus-host interactions remain largely unknown in northern soils outside the growing season. Here, we analyzed the diversity and activity of viruses in oroarctic tundra soils during wintertime using metatranscriptomics. Through de novo virus prediction as well as targeted searches, we identified 995 viral operational taxonomic units (vOTUs) in total. Most of these vOTUs, 93%, represented RNA viruses, part of which were presumably segments of multipartite genomes. RNA vOTUs were classified mainly within the phyla Lenarviricota (259), Kitrinoviricota (198), Pisuviricota (135), Ambiviricota (103), Negarnaviricota (79), and Duplornaviricota (42). Thirty-seven DNA vOTUs (mostly Caudoviricetes) were also detected, suggesting active viral infections. In total, 81% of all vOTUs were assigned with a putative host organism, mostly fungi (515 vOTUs). Viral communities were distinct across vegetation types, and pH and moisture contributed to the differences. Putative novel clades within Ambiviricota and Orpoviricetes were identified, expanding their known diversity. The study contributes to uncovering diverse RNA viruses and viroid-like elements in Arctic tundra soils and highlights that soil viruses remain active in wintertime.

Title: Tailocin as an alternative weapon to type VI secretion system in bee gut symbionts
Authors: Song, Y.; Nikaeen, N.; Kambar, N.; Jones, K. R.; Wade, M.; Leal, C.; Moran, N. A.
Abstract: Antagonistic interactions often shape microbial communities, as co-residents compete for resources. One system of interbacterial antagonism involves tailocins: phage tail-like particles produced by some bacteria to kill close relatives. Their roles in natural communities are poorly studied. Here, we identified putative tailocin loci ubiquitously present in genomes of Snodgrassella species, core members of the bee gut microbiota. We purified tailocins from culture supernatants of different Snodgrassella strains and found that these inhibited growth of multiple Snodgrassella strains but not of strains of other species that cooccur in bee guts. Proteomic analyses corroborated the production of tailocins, and cryogenic electron microscopy imaging revealed their morphology and killing activity via membrane disruption. We generated single- and double-gene knockout mutants of a predator Snodgrassella strain that naturally possesses both tailocin and a type VI secretion system (T6SS) that was previously shown to function in intraspecies competition in bee guts. These mutants were used in tests for antagonism against a prey Snodgrassella strain in vivo. Co-inoculations within gnotobiotic honeybees including visualization within guts showed that both tailocin and T6SS are important for Snodgrassella in intraspecies competition. Each of these two antagonism mechanisms inhibits the establishment of susceptible strains within the ileum. Outcomes depend on the timing of colonization by competing strains, with both tailocin and T6SS giving a stronger advantage when the producing strain colonizes first. Thus, tailocin production can underlie priority effects that have been widely observed in the bee gut community and other host-associated bacterial communities.

Title: An Integrated Miniaturized Metabologenomics Workflow for High-Throughput Actinomycetes Prioritization
Authors: Ouchene, R.; Falquet, L.; Poirel, L.; Allard, P.-M.
Abstract: Antibiotic resistance is a growing global health threat, while the discovery of new antimicrobial agents remains constrained by labor-intensive cultivation, extraction, and screening workflows. We developed a miniaturized, high-throughput metabologenomics workflow integrating Duetz system-based microfermentation, extraction-free UHPLC-HRMS/MS profiling, antibacterial screening, and genome mining. A collection of 80 soil-derived actinomycetes was screened against clinically relevant pathogens, identifying seven isolates active against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), Enterococcus faecium, or both. All isolates were cultivated in Duetz system-based microfermentation plates, and cell-free culture filtrates were analyzed directly by UHPLC-HRMS/MS without solvent extraction. Compared with a conventional workflow, the approach reduced culture-medium consumption by approximately 99%, decreased recurring consumable costs by approximately 96%, and reduced the time required to obtain LC-MS-ready samples from typically 5 days to approximately 20 min. Integration of antibacterial, metabolomic, and genomic datasets supported the annotation of diverse metabolite families, including actinomycins, polyether ionophores, ansamycins, angucyclines, hydroxamate siderophores, ectoines, tambromycin-associated metabolites, and putative lydicamycin metabolites. Selected annotations were validated using commercial standards. Overall, this study demonstrates that integrating miniaturized Duetz system-based cultivation, extraction-free metabolomics, antibacterial screening, and genome mining provides a scalable, robust, and cost-effective platform for high-throughput strain prioritization and natural product discovery.

Title: Crossfeeding interactions in a minimal marine chitin-degrading community
Authors: Haavisto, V.; Sauer, U.
Abstract: Communities of heterotrophic particle-associated marine bacteria contribute to oceanic carbon cycling through interspecies interactions that can influence polysaccharide degradation. While these interactions have been extensively studied using single natural isolates or pairwise combinations thereof, their mechanistic relevance within multispecies communities remains unclear. To address this gap, we developed MCC4, a minimal chitin-degrading bacterial community consisting of two chitin degraders and two non-degrading isolates that represent globally prevalent marine bacterial taxa. We show that the community remains stable across ten growth-dilution cycles, establishing a reproducible model for controlled multi-isolate experiments. Using transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses combined with metabolite supplementation assays, we uncovered the underlying crossfeeding network. While one degrader drives chitin degradation, the other exploits chitin monomers and chitooligomers generated by the main degrader. The two non-degraders are sustained by consuming deacetylated chitin monomers, 2-carbon compounds, nucleotides, and branched-chain amino acids, likely released by degraders. Community assembly is driven by competitive scavenging abilities, potentially complemented by specific survival strategies such as increased motility and deployment of type VI secretion systems. Despite its simplicity, MCC4 captures dynamic microbial interactions characteristic of natural marine ecosystems. It offers a tractable, reproducible framework for investigating how environmental perturbations impact community function and testing ecological theories in particle-associated marine environments.

Title: Preclinical Development and Safety of Laterally Spreading Dual AAV.SPR-MYO7A Vectors for the Treatment of Usher Syndrome Type 1B
Authors: Calabro, K. R.; Andres-Mateos, E.; Kozlowski, C.; Nemec, P. S.; Xu, E. M.; Crosson, S. M.; Fajardo, D.; Friend, H. L.; Peterson, J. J.; Li, W.; Zhang, H.; Sweeney, H. L.; Stevenson, V.; Rind, H.; Leahy, M.; Boyd, R. F.; Boye, S. L.; Boye, S. E.
Abstract: Usher syndrome type 1B (USH1B), caused by mutations in MYO7A, is the most severe form of Usher syndrome and accounts for more than 50% of USH1 cases. Affected patients are born profoundly deaf with vestibular dysfunction and develop progressive retinitis pigmentosa, for which no approved treatment exists. The MYO7A coding sequence exceeds the packaging capacity of adeno-associated virus (AAV), the gold standard vector for retinal gene therapy. To overcome this, we developed dual AAV hybrid and overlap platforms to reconstitute full-length MYO7A expression in photoreceptors and retinal pigment epithelium. Modification of cDNA split points, and reduction of non-coding sequence yielded optimized vector pairs that produced higher full-length MYO7A levels with substantially reduced truncated protein. Packaging in the laterally spreading AAV.SPR capsid enabled supraphysiological MYO7A expression in cynomolgus macaques at macular and distal retinal sites without requiring foveal detachment, an important safety consideration for USH1B patients with remaining central vision. A six-month GLP toxicology study confirmed that ATSN-301, an AAV.SPR-based dual vector reconstituting MYO7A driven by the smCBA promoter, was well tolerated at all doses, with a No Observed Adverse Effect Level established at 1.2E11 vg/eye, supporting its clinical advancement for USH1B.

Title: IG-28 enables identification and quantification of high-confidence isoforms from large bulk and single-cell full-length cDNA datasets
Authors: Calicchio, A.; Li, A. O.; Herwadkar, T.; Mekonen, H. E.; Vollmers, C.
Abstract: The technology to sequence full-length transcriptomes from bulk and single-cell samples has rapidly advanced. As a result, full-length cDNA datasets now reach billions of reads in size which is beyond the capability of most established isoform identification tools. Here, we introduce IG-28 which addresses this challenge with its capability to process and analyze large fl-cDNA datasets fast and using minimal computational resources. In contrast to its predecessor Mandalorion, IG-28 is not limited to bulk fl-cDNA but is capable of parsing, processing, and analyzing single-cell fl-cDNA datasets. It does so in a lightweight, flexible manner, integrating seamlessly with established scRNA-seq analysis workflows. We benchmarked IG-28 against a variety of established and new isoform identification tools using several bulk and a complex single-cell fl-cDNA dataset and found that IG-28 consistently outperformed the other tools by identifying high-confidence public isoforms.

Title: Arena3D 3.0: a web server for exploring, analyzing, annotating and sharing multilayered networks in 3D
Authors: Karatzas, E.; Baltoumas, F.; Kokoli, M.; Galaras, A.; Aplakidou, E.; Itsios, M.; Chasapi, I. N.; Chasapi, M. N.; Lamari, E.; Georgakopoulos-Soares, I.; Przulj, N.; Pavlopoulos, G. A.
Abstract: Multilayer networks describe biological entities linked by several kinds of relation or measured under several conditions. Arena3D 3.0, a complete reimplementation of Arena3Dweb, gives each layer its own place in an interactive 3D scene. Networks are uploaded or imported from STRING, IntAct, OmniPath, NDEx, Reactome and the Gene Ontology. Twelve layouts, seven in 3D, are available, and node copies can be aligned across layers. Layers are drawn as floors or 3D containers in thirteen arrangements, including 3D hive plots. Communities and annotated groups can be laid out apart and outlined as hulls or fog clouds, and edges can be bundled. Analyses cover node and multilayer metrics, distributions and perturbation, with chord, Sankey, heatmap, UpSet and UMAP views. Networks go to Cytoscape, Gephi Lite, NORMA and JBrowse 2, gene lists to Flame, and a REST API gives programmatic access. Arena3D 3.0 is free at www.arena3d.org without login.

Title: Rugnux: from diffraction images to structure at synchrotrons and XFELs in one program
Authors: Leonarski, F.; Wang, M.
Abstract: Rising data rates in macromolecular crystallography outpace multi-program pipelines on computing clusters. Rugnux, a single GPU-accelerated program, turns rotation or serial still diffraction images into merged data and an initial structure. At synchrotrons, results arrive seconds after the last image; on one workstation, 207 public datasets from 36 sources took a median of 15 s each, with deposition-quality. Serial XFEL data were processed faster than the collection rate, enabling real-time structure determination.

Title: Co-transcriptomic network analysis of host-parasite interactions reveals genes underpinning parasite fitness
Authors: Inskeep, T.; Celis, E.; Nguyen, A. K.; Groen, S. C.
Abstract: Interactions between parasites and their host organisms generate continuous variation in infection outcomes. Although dual transcriptome studies have demonstrated extensive molecular dialogues between interacting species, it is still unclear how natural variation in host and parasite gene regulatory networks and coordination between them contribute to diverse disease phenotypes. Here, we re-contextualized co-transcriptomes from recombinant inbred lines of the plant-parasitic root-knot nematode Meloidogyne hapla infecting Medicago truncatula host plants with relative measures of infection intensity as a proxy for parasite load. We used infection intensity to estimate interaction gradients on gene expression by calculating its covariance with transcript levels. Quantitative analyses of interaction gradients for host and parasite transcriptomes identified major differences in development-related transcriptional programs along the infection continuum. In addition, integrated network analyses connected host cell wall remodeling with parasite protein production and secretion. Silencing of candidate root-knot nematode genes reduced host galling and parasite reproductive fitness, providing experimental support for our network-derived predictions. Together, our findings present an integrated systems genetics framework connecting naturally occurring genetic variation to quantitative disease phenotypes.

Title: Dengue Virus Serotype 2 Infection Transcriptionally Reprograms Host Neutrophils to Establish an Immunosuppressive Microenvironment in Mice
Authors: Rawat, S.; Chhetri, A.; Nimesh, S.; Pandey, A. D.; Sadhu, S.; Siddqui, G.; Samal, S.; Awasthi, A.; Banerjee, A.
Abstract: Dengue virus (DV) infection triggers profound alterations in host immune responses, yet the transcriptomic reprogramming of innate immune cells during disease progression remains incompletely understood. Here, we demonstrated that Dengue virus serotype 2 (DV-2) infection transcriptionally reprograms host neutrophils, establishing an immunosuppressive microenvironment that facilitates pathogenesis. Through scRNA transcriptomic profiling of bone marrow and spleen cells from the DV-2-infected AG129 mouse model, we delineated a distinct neutrophil signature that shows dynamic shifts in immature and activated populations over the course of dengue infection. We also characterized a specific Ly6Glow subpopulation, notably Fibrinogen-like protein 2 (FGL2)-expressing subsets, that appeared with disease progression. Serum FGL2 levels were significantly elevated in both DV-2-infected mice and human dengue-positive patients. Furthermore, treatment of splenocytes with FGL2 or FGL2-enriched neutrophil secretomes suppressed T cell functional activity and promoted an immunosuppressive phenotype. Together, these findings reveal how DV-2-driven neutrophil reprogramming shapes an immunosuppressive network, highlighting the importance of studying FGL2-expressing neutrophil subsets to understand dengue immunopathogenesis.

Title: The influence of drug dosing regimen on extinction and adaptation during experimental evolution in Candida albicans
Authors: Sethi, P.; Pouteau, E.; Sumanarathnea, A.; Gerstein, A.
Abstract: The antifungal azole drug fluconazole (FLC) is frequently prescribed for treating Candida albicans infections. Azole drugs are typically fungistatic; they inhibit cell growth rather than kill susceptible cells within a population. Therefore, fungal populations can adapt to fluconazole through increased drug resistance or increased drug tolerance (the ability of a subpopulation of susceptible cells to grow slowly at inhibitory drug concentrations). To our knowledge, no prior experiments have examined how different factors influence extinction propensity, although previous in vitro studies show that both drug concentration and strain background can influence adaptation. To determine how the drug dosing regimen, namely fluconazole concentration and transfer duration (i.e., the amount of time between transfer into fresh medium), influenced extinction and adaptation in Candida albicans, we conducted a fully factorial series of short in vitro evolution experiments. Dosing regimen significantly influenced extinction: all replicates evolved at all drug concentrations survived the 48 h and 72 h transfer experiments, yet the extinction rate increased sharply from low to high drug concentration with 24 h transfers. Increases in drug tolerance were frequent regardless of the dosing regimen. In contrast, drug resistance and growth rate both tended to decrease following evolution at higher drug concentrations. Fluconazole-evolved replicates exhibited frequent increases in cross-tolerance and decreases in cross-resistance in a panel of other azole drugs. Genome size changes were common in some strain backgrounds evolved to higher fluconazole concentrations, regardless of transfer times. Combined, our results indicate that many experimental factors can influence the trajectory of adaptation, and show that extinction in a fungistatic drug occurs readily at high drug concentrations with rapid transfers.

Title: A droplet-to-data workflow for antimicrobial screening of complex matrices
Authors: Sanka, I.; Vaher, M.; Setiawibawa, A. A.; Saar-Reismaa, P.; Pata, P.; Ruuson, K.; Scheler, O.; Bartkova, S.
Abstract: Screening plant extracts and other complex natural matrices for antibacterial activity is complicated by optical interference and population averaging in conventional bulk assays. Droplet-based assays mitigate interference while enabling high-throughput assessment of bacterial subpopulations. However, analyzing the resulting image data involves difficult image processing, classification, and interpretation. Here, we present a democratized workflow for antimicrobial screening in complex matrices that combines a polydisperse droplet-based assay with EasyFlow 2.0 (EF2), our updated droplet image analysis platform. EF2 offers stable containerized deployment, expanded polydisperse droplet support, automated thresholding and MIC estimation, LLM-assisted data exploration, and import of other software outputs such as CellProfiler (CP) measurements and CellProfiler Analyst (CPA) classification models. As proof of concept, we applied this workflow to assess the antibacterial and aggregation-modulating effects of chemically distinct extracts of Taraxacum officinale, Rhodiola rosea, and Lonicera caerulea against Escherichia coli. Extracts were chemically characterized by HPLC-MS and evaluated using both standard 96-well plate microdilution and droplet-based assays. In total, 27,059 droplets were segmented in CP, classified into four growth phenotypes using a CPA random forest model, and analyzed in EF2. The droplet-based assay reached minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) at lower extract concentrations than 96-well plate microdilution and revealed extract-specific aggregation effects: L. caerulea reduced E. coli aggregation, whereas T. officinale did not. R. rosea reduced growth in the 96-well plate microdilution assay, but high concentrations caused droplet gelation that prevented droplet-based analysis, showing that sample components must be checked for compatibility with droplet formation. These results illustrate that the EF2-centered workflow supports rapid, automated MIC estimation through unsupervised thresholding when labels are unavailable, and four-class aggregation phenotyping when a CPA model is supplied. This workflow offers flexible, scalable screening, potentially extendable beyond plant extracts to other complex sample matrices.

Title: A portable C-terminal rheostat calibrates RecE/Redα exonuclease activity for enhanced bacterial recombineering
Authors: Luan, J.; Jiang, C.; Guo, R.; Wang, C.; Wang, S.; Stewart, A. F.; Fu, J.; Zhang, Y.; Wang, H.
Abstract: Recombineering enables precise genome engineering across diverse bacteria, yet efficient tools for large DNA integration remain underdeveloped for Streptomyces and other biotechnologically relevant bacteria. Here we identify a panel of highly active RecET recombinase pairs from actinobacteriophages that mediate efficient homologous recombination in Streptomyces. The lead candidate, Che9cRecET, supports genomic integration of kilobase-scale DNA with only 50bp homology arms and enables accurate insertion of 79kb biosynthetic gene clusters, far outperforming conventional genome editing approaches. Structural and biochemical analyses reveal Che9cRecE as a distinct C3-symmetric toroidal homotrimeric 5'-3' exonuclease, whose extended C-terminal loop acts as a tunable rheostat calibrating exonuclease activity to an optimal window for recombination. We further show this portable C-terminal loop enhances recombineering efficiency across phylogenetically diverse exonucleases including Escherichia coli Redalpha/RecE and Pseudomonas A. Our work uncovers a conserved regulatory mechanism of the RecE/Redalpha exonuclease family and delivers a generalizable strategy for advancing bacterial genome editing.

Title: Endonuclease G governs an antiviral RNA surveillance system in budding yeast
Authors: Gao, J.; Remnant, B.; Martyn, B.; Chung, M.; Li, J.; Pickett, M.; Chau, S.; Bayfield, M. A.; Meneghini, M. D.
Abstract: Endonuclease G family DNA/RNA nucleases localize to the mitochondrial intermembrane space and prevent escape of mitochondrial DNA to the cytosol or nucleus. While extramitochondrial Endonuclease G also targets nuclear DNA during cell death, RNA regulatory roles of this family remain enigmatic. Here we discover an RNA surveillance system in Saccharomyces cerevisiae governed by Nuc1, the yeast Endonuclease G homolog. This system limits replication of L-A, an RNA mycovirus that endemically infects this organism. Whereas L-A resides in the cytosol, we find that Nuc1's antiviral function requires its mitochondrial intermembrane space localization. To understand Nuc1's indirect antiviral mechanism we investigated its genetic interactions with REX1 and REX2, RNA exonucleases that control 3' end processing of tRNA and rRNA intermediates in the nucleus. We demonstrate that the nuc1{triangleup} antiviral defect is massively amplified by rex1{triangleup} rex2{triangleup} leading to L-A RNA levels that surpass mature rRNAs and overwhelm the cells. NUC1 concurrently controls a pool of mis-processed tRNA and rRNA species that accumulate in rex1{triangleup} rex2{triangleup} mutants. Linking these mis-processed RNAs with L-A control, we show they are significantly reduced in L-A infected cells, suggesting that L-A depletes them to enhance its replication. Our findings identify a previously unrecognized RNA surveillance function of Nuc1 that prevents aberrant rRNA and tRNA species from promoting replication of the L-A mycovirus.

Title: STRIPAK associates with Rabex5-Rabaptin5 to promote Rab5-dependent early endosome formation and EGFR transport
Authors: Woodman, P.; Francavilla, C.; Sugar, S. N.; Wunderley, L.; Trotter, E. W.; Shimizu, H.; Parkinson, G.; Fullwood, P.
Abstract: His Domain Protein Tyrosine Phosphatase (HD-PTP) is required for multivesicular body (MVB) formation and endosome maturation, with Rab5-GTP levels raised upon HD-PTP depletion (Parkinson et al., 2021. doi: 10/1242/jcs.259192). Mass Spectrometry-based interactomics revealed that HD-PTP depletion increased association of Rabaptin5, a component of the early endosome Rabex5-Rabaptin5 Rab5-GEF, with multiple components of STRIPAK (striatin-interacting phosphatase and kinase). Native IPs and co-expression studies confirmed association between STRIPAK and Rabex5-Rabaptin5, including Strip1-Rabex5 and SLMAP-Rabaptin5 interactions. Consistent with functional Rabaptin5-STRIPAK links, co-depletion of Strip1 or Rabaptin5 with HD-PTP restored normal early endosome positioning and Rab5 distribution. Strip1 depletion impaired formation of central, Rab5-positive early endosomes, reduced cellular Rab5-GTP levels, and prevented the accumulation of internalised EGF-EGFR into centrally located endosomes. SLMAP depletion accentuated the central clustering of early endosomes and other endosomal compartments while also retarding the generation of new, EGFR-containing endosomes and EGFR lysosomal transport. We conclude that STRIPAK is a novel co-assembly factor of Rabex5-Rabaptin5, exerting subunit-specific effects on early endosomes.

Title: Standardisation Challenges in ELISA-Based Quantification of Equine Chorionic Gonadotropin (eCG/PMSG)
Authors: Mishchenko, P.; Martinez, R. M.; Buch, T.; Loesle, M.
Abstract: Equine chorionic gonadotropin (eCG/PMSG) is widely used for female-cycle synchronization and estrus induction in livestock and in biomedical research, where reliable quantitative assessment is increasingly important. However, its structural and glycosylation heterogeneity complicates antibody-based measurement and assay standardization. This Technical Note evaluated six commercially available quantitative PMSG ELISA kits representing three distinct analytical profile groups. Kit-provided calibration standards were characterized by Western blotting, Coomassie staining, and LC-MS/MS, while quantitative performance was assessed using serial dilutions of two commercial PMSG preparations. DRG, Creative Diagnostics, and Demeditec showed similar calibration-standard profiles and concentration-dependent responses, although measured concentrations were consistently below nominal values. Biomatik and MyBiosource displayed closely related analytical profiles but little meaningful concentration-dependent response, whereas Krishgen measurements remained within a narrow range despite changes in nominal PMSG input. The calibration standards differed substantially in protein composition, and no eCG-derived peptides were identified by LC-MS/MS under the conditions used. These findings demonstrate that quantitative results obtained with commercially available PMSG ELISAs are not necessarily comparable and may be strongly influenced by calibration-material composition, assay format, and matrix effects. The findings highlight the limitations of current quantitative PMSG assays and the need for a well-characterized, commutable reference material, together with assay-specific validation of dilution parallelism and analyte recovery, to improve the reliability and comparability of eCG/PMSG measurements.

Title: Few-shot regulatory sequence design with a genomic language model
Authors: Hie, B.; Hao, Y. A.; Liu, M.; Nori, D.; Brixi, G.; Lau, T.; Ramakrishnan, C. A.; Chang, D.; Park, R.; Allen, W. E.
Abstract: A central challenge in generative biology is translating knowledge learned from natural sequences and experiments into designs with desired functions. In-context learning (ICL) is an emergent capability of large language models that allows them to adapt to new tasks from a few examples without additional training, enabling these models to become general-purpose learners. Here, we show that the genome language model, Evo 2, exhibits generative ICL in biological sequence design. Prompting with just tens of examples conditions Evo 2 to generate novel and diverse regulatory DNA sequences without any additional training. Mechanistic analysis suggests that genomic ICL may originate from induction, similar to phenomena observed in natural language. Reinforcement learning leveraging sequence-to-function models as experiment-derived rewards further strengthens ICL. We first validate this approach by generating enhancers that drive cell-type-specific gene expression in three human cell lines. Extending this approach in vivo, enhancers designed using human regulatory element data selectively label layer 5 extratelencephalic neurons in the mouse cortex with high specificity and stronger activity than existing enhancers. Our study provides evidence of emergent properties in genomic sequence models and introduces a promising approach for improving functional conditioning in generative biology.

Title: Biosynthetic additive manufacturing through mycelium-bacteria consortia
Authors: Yuan, H.; Heller, L. J. J.; Xing, Y.; Wang, L.; Huang, J.; Nguyen, K.; Cai, Y.; Waller, B.; Chen, C.; Hubbard, G.; Yong, R.; DelPlace, E.; Belo, M.; Manosh, S.; Inamdar, S.; Shan, X.; Zang, X.; Huang, J.; Li, T.; Bonito, G.; Lan, K.; Li, J.
Abstract: Lignocellulosic biomass is the most abundant renewable raw material on Earth, yet its structural and carbon-storage potential remains unrealized: microbial decomposition returns stored carbon to the atmosphere before it can be harnessed as a durable material. Distinct microbial processes, such as biosynthesis and biomineralization, offer a natural counterpoint, converting organic carbon into mechanically robust, persistent materials such as polymers and minerals. Here, we establish a biosynthetic additive manufacturing strategy through mycelium-bacteria consortia, by coupling fungal self-assembly with bacterial biomineralization inside fabricated three-dimensional scaffolds derived from lignocellulosic biomass. Trametes versicolor forms a continuous living mycelial network that serves as both a structural template and a transport pathway, guiding the spatial colonization of Sporosarcina pasteurii and enabling volumetric calcium carbonate deposition throughout the scaffold interior, overcoming the surface-limited mineralization of conventional microbial systems. Integration with helicoidal Bouligand architectures translates microscale mineral reinforcement into macroscale performance, increasing compressive Young's modulus by 7-14-fold and ultimate strength by 5-fold relative to unmineralized conventional mycelium-based living composites. The living mycelial network also enables autonomous self-healing and modular self-assembly through hyphal bridging without external adhesives or energy input. This work establishes a scalable route for converting and upcycling transient biomass carbon into durable living structural materials for sustainable construction.

Title: Mesoscale Soft Robotics for Mechanically Perturbing and Functionally Monitoring Responses in Human Organoids
Authors: Maeng, W.-Y.; Lv, Z.; Samei, Y.; Ha, K.-H.; Kim, K. S.; Prabakar, L. P.; Chychula, I. A.; Iyer, V.; Li, B.; Mao, Y.; Xu, S.; Park, T. W.; Li, S.; Holgren, C. W.; Jo, Y. J.; Ahn, H.-Y.; Liu, N.; Yoo, S.; Oh, S.; Koo, J.; McNally, E. M.; Efimov, I. R.; Fullenkamp, D. E.; Huang, Y.; Finan, J. D.; Rogers, J. A.
Abstract: Human organoids represent promising models for studies of significance to the biology and medical communities. Of the existing approaches for monitoring organoids, none offers the ability to apply programmable mechanical forces while simultaneously recording multi-modal physiological responses, of relevance to phenomena spanning from traumatic brain injuries to cardiac rhythm disorders. Here, we present a mesoscale soft robotic organoid interface that enables programmable delivery of forces to organoids of diverse shapes, and to map electrophysiological activity and mechanical responses. The platform combines actuation elements with integrated sensors for quantitative measurement and control. Studies using this technology reveal that spheroidal cortical organoids exhibit distinct responses to mechanical trauma, including silencing, recovery, and changes in neuronal firing patterns. Additional experiments on cardiac ring tissues demonstrate that sustained stretching induces beat-to-beat rhythm variability and altered conduction. The results establish a framework for investigating force-triggered transitions between physiological and disease-like states in human tissue models.

Title: IOP-independent treatment for neurodegeneration in glaucoma using optimized ROS-scavenging microparticles for sustained release of erythropoietin
Authors: DeJulius, C.; Naguib, S.; Poley, P.; Rasdall, M.; Dean, T.; Conner, A.; D'Empaire-Salomon, S.; Hardin, R.; Artis, E.; d'Arcy, R.; Carlson, B.; Calkins, D.; Duvall, C.; Rex, T. S.
Abstract: Glaucoma is a slow-progressing neurodegenerative disease of the optic projection to the brain and a leading cause of blindness worldwide. Current treatments are targeted towards lowering intraocular pressure (IOP), the only known, modifiable risk factor; however, this strategy is ineffective in many patients. An early hallmark of glaucomatous neurodegeneration is increased reactive oxygen species (ROS), representing an alternative opportunity for intervention to halt or slow disease progression. In this work, we optimize a ROS-scavenging copolymer, poly(propylene sulfide-co-ethylene sulfide) (PPSES), for formulation of size-controlled, stabilized, antioxidant microparticles (MPs) for sustained release of the protein erythropoietin (EPO). EPO promotes biological antioxidant defense via activation of NRF2-mediated transcription of antioxidant genes. This MP system overcomes the short half-life of EPO and leverages the combined benefits of bioactive EPO with long-lasting, inherently antioxidant PPSES MPs. The lead EPO-MP formulation preserves neurons in both mouse and non-human primate models of glaucoma through suppression of oxidative stress and optic nerve degeneration. EPO-loaded PPSES MPs represent a translationally relevant therapy for long-term management of glaucoma independent of IOP.

Title: Carrier-Limited Release Risk in Electrospun Nanofibers for Regenerative Endodontics: Constraint Discovery from 25 Formulations
Authors: Brimo, N.; Serdaroglu, D. C.
Abstract: Regenerative endodontics needs an intracanal carrier that keeps disinfecting across a dressing interval that clinicians schedule at one to four weeks, without harming the stem cells that rebuild the pulp. We ask what one completed 25-formulation electrospinning campaign of poly(vinylpyrrolidone) (PVP) fibers carrying metronidazole, ciprofloxacin, minocycline and Ca(OH)2 can decide, and use machine learning for constraint discovery and decision support rather than as a new predictor. After an audit against the source thesis, logistic regression predicts fine-fiber formation at 96% leave-one-out accuracy, but a one-threshold rule does as well, the gain over the 80% majority baseline is not significant (exact McNemar p = 0.125), and accuracy falls to 84% when mixture loading is encoded per component. Diameter models interpolate within formulation families (ridge MAE 193 nm, 95% CI 96 to 317 nm) and fail across them (R^2 < 0). Because the campaign never measured release, we assemble a same-drug, cross-carrier evidence table: 17 bounded metronidazole and ciprofloxacin observations from seven studies, with two-sided censoring. Water-soluble carriers (PVP, PVA) completed release within 80 h (PVP within 8 h); no water-insoluble monolithic carrier reached 90% within its observation window, releasing 1.5 to 50%; both within-study comparisons separate at matched loading; and blend, core-shell and thick-mat architectures released over 3 to 28 days. The PVP mats therefore carry a carrier-limited release risk, not a proven ceiling, and one dissolution experiment can confirm or overturn it. A censoring-aware screen keeps three necessarily and one possibly nondominated formulation, and fixed-budget replays show that uncertainty sampling finds failed formulations sooner, except the one it is confidently wrong about.

Title: Dietary fibre responses emerge through host-dietary regime interplay: Apple pectin modulates immune reactivity in adult zebrafish
Authors: Abi Assaf, J.; Le Gall, G.; Sullivan, R.; Bezrucico-Pyatakov, A.; Carlsson, H.; Cohen-Krais, J.; de Coriolis, J.-C.; Godden, A. M.; Marcu, D.; Gorton, D.; Immler, S.
Abstract: Dietary fibres are rarely consumed independently. Instead, they form part of an overall diet that includes dietary fibres from different sources, in varying amounts and consumed under different feeding patterns. Here, we tested how dietary regimes containing apple pectin, oat {beta}-glucan, or cellulose shaped the host. We analysed gut microbiome composition by 16S rRNA sequencing, measured brain and intestinal SCFA profiles by targeted metabolomics, and assessed immunomodulation by measuring gene expression systemically in the blood and locally in the spleen, as well as intestinal enzyme activity. The dietary intervention was conducted for 12 weeks on adult female and male zebrafish (Danio rerio). Our results show that the gut microbial composition can be relatively stable across different dietary fibre exposure patterns yet still vary significantly between the sexes. Additionally, the effect of sex on the gut microbiome may become more evident when dietary fibres are administered at high dosages, but intermittently. Dietary fibre regimes can alter intestinal short-chain fatty acid profiles more readily than brain profiles, which show a stronger sexually dimorphic response. Interestingly, apple pectin modulated the zebrafish immune response through interactions dependent on the overall regime, tissue, sex, and host immune status. Notably, tissue il1b gene expression differed depending on how apple pectin was administered and the host's physiological state. Collectively, our study emphasises the highly context-specific effects of dietary fibres, shaped by the dynamic interplay between the overall dietary regime and intertwined host factors.

Title: Abundance-weighted analysis and deep functional metagenomic selection reveals unrecognized diversity of soil-derived streptothricin acetyltransferases
Authors: Yang, L.; Crofts, T. S.
Abstract: Streptothricins (STCs) are broad-spectrum antibiotics under investigation for their therapeutic potential against antibiotic-resistant Gram-negative pathogens. However, the extent and diversity of genes that confer resistance to STCs, or their environmental resistome, remains largely unknown and is essentially limited to a handful of STC acetyltransferases. Here, we used a deep functional metagenomic approach to uncover previously unrecognized STC resistance determinants. A functional metagenomic library containing ca. 700 Gigabases of soil metagenomic DNA was selected for resistance to nourseothricin (NTC), a mixture of STC congeners, resulting in collection and sequencing of nearly 30,000 resistant clones. An abundance-weighted sequence analysis identified 265 acetyltransferase-like candidates spanning broad phylogenetic, taxonomic, and genomic diversity. Re-cloning and experimental testing of 18 candidates chosen to cover acetyltransferase sequence space confirmed that 10 conferred significant NTC resistance in Escherichia coli. Phylogenetic analyses identified three previously uncharacterized STC acetyltransferase lineages, designated as SatC, SatD, and SatE. Despite substantial sequence divergence from characterized streptothricin acetyltransferases (maximum amino acid identities of approximately 31% for SatC and SatD and up to 47.5% for SatE), these enzymes largely retained key residues associated with streptothricin binding and catalysis. In addition to strongly increasing NTC resistance, expression of the SatC construct in E. coli also significantly decreased susceptibility to the aminoglycoside antibiotics amikacin and kanamycin. Together, these findings reveal a substantially broader than previously known environmental repertoire of STC acetyltransferases and demonstrate how deep functional metagenomic selections, combined with abundance-weighted hit calling, phylogenetic analysis, and structural prediction, can uncover novel resistance functions.

Title: Integrative multi-omics decoding of the host response to Klebsiella pneumoniae infection reveals an itaconate-centred metabolic-immune axis and a spatially organised inflammatory programme
Authors: Zhao, Y.; Cheng, H.; Zhou, S.; He, L.; Xiu, C.; Huang, B.; Lu, X.
Abstract: Background: Klebsiella pneumoniae (Kp) is a leading cause of hospital and community acquired pneumonia and bacteraemia, and hypervirulent and carbapenem resistant lineages continue to expand worldwide. Although individual omics layers of Kp infection have been profiled, the host-level molecular logic that connects transcriptional, cellular, metabolic and spatial programmes has not been systematically integrated. Methods: We curated 16 public datasets spanning four modalities-bulk and dual host pathogen RNA-seq (six datasets; 118 libraries), single-cell RNA-seq (four datasets; {approx}164,000 cells), untargeted/targeted metabolomics (four datasets; 1,842 molecular features) and Visium spatial transcriptomics (two datasets; {approx}11,400 spots) covering murine lung infection models, hypervirulent and classical Kp strains, carbapenem-resistant isolates and human clinical specimens. Datasets were harmonised through a standardised pipeline (Salmon/DESeq2; Scanpy/Harmony; MetaboAnalyst; RCTD/spacexr), and integrated by WGCNA, GSVA, CellChat, Monocle3, SCENIC, joint-pathway analysis, RCTD deconvolution, and machine-learning feature selection (LASSO, random forest, SVM-RFE, XGBoost) with 1,000x bootstrap internal validation and independent external validation. Results: Kp infection evoked a coherent 920 gene neutrophil inflammatory response ({approx}520 up-/{approx}400 down-regulated genes) dominated by IL-17/TNF/NF-{kappa}B signalling, neutrophil degranulation, HIF-1-linked glycolysis and itaconate biosynthesis. A turquoise co-expression module (r = 0.86 with infection status) yielded a ten-gene hub signature (IRG1, S100A9, IL1B, CXCL2, SLC7A11, HMOX1, PTGS2, NFKBIA, LST1, FCGR3B). Single-cell profiling resolved twelve major lung lineages and eleven myeloid substates, tracing a Monocle3 trajectory from Cxcr2hi inflammatory neutrophils through an Irg1/Slc7a11hi oxidative phase into Cxcr4hi/Trem2hi suppressive states; CellChat identified S100A8/A9-TLR4 and CXCL2-CXCR2 as the most amplified axes (8.5x and 4.2x). Metabolomics revealed 30-fold pulmonary itaconate accumulation together with succinate and lactate elevation, glucose/glutamine depletion and glutathione collapse, and joint-pathway analysis positioned the TCA-cycle itaconate and ferroptosis modules as the strongest convergent perturbations. Spatial transcriptomics mapped these programmes onto five anatomical niches, with IRG1 expression peaking in the infection core (58% neutrophil content) and declining radially. A ten-gene host-response classification model reached AUC=0.958 in discovery, 0.937 in internal validation and 0.884-0.912 in two independent external cohorts (Brier score 0.071). Conclusions: By vertically integrating public multi-omics data, we define an itaconate-centred metabolic-immune axis that couples inflammatory myeloid expansion to spatially segregated metabolic niches, and we deliver a validated host-side molecular signature that discriminates Kp infection from non-infected states.

Title: A single-plane electrical impedance tomography framework for integrated liver and kidney assessment
Authors: Wu, A.; Lai, J.-C.; Ho, M. K.; Ge, J. Q. J.; Gong, N.-j.; Zhou, I. Y.; Wong, M.; Edelman, B. J.; Chan, R. W.
Abstract: Chronic liver and kidney diseases frequently coexist, but their assessment typically requires separate clinical workflows involving serum-based estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) testing and liver elastography-based controlled attenuation parameter (CAP). Electrical impedance tomography (EIT) has recently shown promise for providing portable, non-invasive proxies for both reference measurements. However, existing multi-organ EIT assessment still requires different acquisition protocols for each organ. To simplify this procedure, we assessed the feasibility of a single-plane EIT framework for reconstructing organ-specific images and estimating liver and kidney health from one abdominal belt placement. Across diverse abdominal belt locations, opposite-plane deviation was significantly greater for eGFREIT estimates (2.92%; IQR, 0.46-12.53%) than for CAPEIT estimates (0.94%; IQR, 0.66-1.70%) (p < 0.01). For both organs, compared to images acquired at the conventional organ-specific planes, image correlation significantly decreased (both, p < 0.05) and normalized root mean squared error significantly increased (both, p < 0.05) at the furthest imaging plane, with these differences being numerically larger for the kidney. Together, these results supported the kidney plane as the preferred location for multi-organ assessment. Test-retest evaluation after belt removal and reapplication demonstrated that the correlation between two repeated CAPEIT estimates was just as strong at the kidney plane (R2 = 0.98, p < 0.001) as it was at the conventional liver plane (R2 = 0.97, p < 0.001). Finally, in an independent clinical cohort, kidney-plane CAPEIT estimates were significantly higher in participants with a high metabolic liver-risk profile (i.e. diabetes and high blood pressure) (p < 0.005). CAPEIT estimates also distinguished high and low metabolic risk groups with an AUC of 0.756. Together, these findings support the feasibility of a portable multi-organ EIT imaging framework capable of extracting complementary liver and kidney information from a single belt placement.

Title: Network analysis reveals converging molecular mechanisms in genetic epilepsies
Authors: Duan, Y.; Valeanu, A.; Rouhl, R. P. W.; Vermeulen, J. R.; de Kok, T. M.; Ehrhart, F.
Abstract: Background: Rare genetic epilepsies are often difficult to diagnose and treat. They can arise from changes in many different genes, and the molecular basis linking these changes to epilepsy remains poorly understood. This complexity makes it difficult to select effective treatments and develop new therapies, leaving many patients with poorly controlled seizures and reduced quality of life Methods: To address this gap, we first identified epilepsy-associated genes and conducted a network-based analysis of biomolecular interactions in genetic epilepsy to identify converging pathways with high translational relevance and potential therapeutic targets. To run the analysis, we constructed a human brain-specific molecular interaction network by integrating all human pathways from the WikiPathways database. HotNet2 was then applied to identify highly perturbed clusters through evidence-based weight diffusion of EAGs in the human brain network. Results: We identified 2,496 epilepsy-associated genes (EAGs) from multiple resources.
