Authors: Gerber, C. M.; Zezza, G.; Guidi, V.; Wyler, M.; Bachofen, C.; Kubacki, J.
Abstract: Switzerland hosts over 400 bird species, many of which are migratory. Through diverse movement patterns, ranging from short distances to almost global migrations, these birds can introduce zoonotic viruses, such as West Nile virus (WNV) or avian influenza virus (AIV), as well as unknown and potentially emerging viruses. Furthermore, they facilitate the global dispersal of infected ectoparasites, particularly ticks, risking the introduction of novel tick-borne diseases. To assess this risk, we sampled 42 bird species (39 migratory, 3 resident) over seven months in 2023 at the Bolle di Magadino nature reserve and the Piano di Magadino area in the canton Ticino (Switzerland). This region, because of its transitional climate, serves as an important resting and breeding ground for migratory birds. In total, 496 oropharyngeal-cloacal swabs, 164 sera, and 22 associated ticks were collected. While RT-qPCR of the swabs detected no active WNV or AIV infections, ELISA testing identified Orthoflavivirus antibodies in 15 of 164 sera, indicating prior exposure. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing revealed a viral landscape spanning 33 families (29 of which were identified in birds). Within this virome, DNA viruses, predominantly Circoviridae, Genomoviridae, and Parvoviridae, dominated in abundance but exhibited low diversity. In contrast, the highly diverse RNA virome primarily reflected the birds dietary habits and the local habitat at the nature reserve. Notably, we report the first detection of Bole tick virus 4 (BoTV4) in Switzerland, identified in several ticks (Rhipicephalus turanicus) associated with long-distance migrants. This member of the newly established Pestiviridae family is already established in parts of Asia, Africa, and Europe. This study provides the first active surveillance of the wild bird virome in Switzerland. Our findings establish a framework for the early detection of emerging viruses and underscore the role of migratory birds as dispersal vectors for ticks and novel tick-borne viruses.

Title: Dynamic evolution of diaphorin biosynthetic genes against a background of genome conservation in Profftella
Authors: Yasuda, Y.; Piel, J.; Malenovsky, I.; Gjonov, I.; Hirose, Y.; Nakabachi, A.
Abstract: The Asian citrus psyllid Diaphorina citri (Insecta: Hemiptera), a major agricultural pest, harbors the unusual obligate bacterial symbiont "Candidatus Profftella armatura" (Profftella), which is intimately integrated with its host yet devotes a remarkably large proportion of its highly reduced genome to the production of diaphorin, a bioactive polyketide. To gain insight into the evolution of this distinctive symbiont, we determined the genomes of Profftella and the co-resident nutritional symbiont "Candidatus Carsonella ruddii" (Carsonella) from Diaphorina lycii and compared them with previously characterized counterparts from D. citri and D. cf. continua. The Profftella and Carsonella chromosomes from D. lycii were 471 and 174 kb, respectively, and Profftella harbored an 8-kb plasmid. Genome organization and gene content were highly conserved across the three lineages. The diaphorin biosynthetic system likewise retained its overall organization, consistent with an important role for diaphorin in the Diaphorina symbiotic system. Remarkably, however, pronounced lineage-specific structural variation was observed in diaphorin synthases DipP and DipT, encoded by two of the 20 diaphorin biosynthetic genes. These synthases contained three extensively amplified tandem arrays of acyl carrier protein (ACP) domains that carry growing polyketide intermediates, with up to seven copies compared with one or two at corresponding positions in the related pederin synthases. All three regions of tandem ACP repeats showed copy-number variation among the Profftella lineages. This variation indicates that ACP amplification remains evolutionarily dynamic despite the otherwise highly constrained symbiotic genome. Together, our findings show that even highly integrated obligate symbionts retain evolutionary flexibility in specialized functional systems.

Title: Single-base mapping of m6A in lncRNAs reveals a distinct landscape linked to transposable elements and RNA processing
Authors: Kwon, E.; Li, Z.; Zhou, C.
Abstract: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most abundant internal RNA modification with established roles in mRNA metabolism. Although m6A has been characterized in several well-known long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs), its transcriptome-wide landscape and roles remain poorly understood. Here, we characterized the m6A landscape of lncRNAs at single-base resolution, identified m6A deposition-associated features, and investigated potential roles of m6A in lncRNA processing. Unlike in mRNAs, m6A sites are broadly distributed along lncRNAs. We further found that these differences in m6A patterns between lncRNAs and mRNAs may reflect contributions from transposable element-derived sequence to motif availability and local RNA structure, together with splicing-related constraints on m6A deposition near exon junctions. Additionally, m6A may be relevant to the regulation of lncRNA polyadenylation. Together, these findings define the single-base-resolution m6A landscape in lncRNAs, and connect lncRNA methylation to transposable elements, RNA structure, splicing, and polyadenylation. This study broadens our understanding of m6A in the lncRNA epitranscriptome.

Title: Development of a multi-organ single-cell atlas of systemic sclerosis reveals shared and tissue-specific pathogenic pathways.
Authors: Iperi, C.; Geiss, C.; Lugar, M.; Stauffer, P.; Vlachogiannis, N.; Hofman, A.; Khmelevskaya, A.; Sfikakis, P. P.; Hoffmann-Vold, A.-M.; Micheroli, R.; Seiler, C.; Distler, O.; Ospelt, C.; Elhai, M.
Abstract: Objectives: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a multi-organ autoimmune disease for which no broadly effective disease-modifying treatment exists. We developed an integrated multi-organ single-cell atlas of SSc to identify shared and organ specific disease-associated transcriptional programmes and potential therapeutic targets. Methods: We integrated single-cell RNA-sequencing data from skin, lung, synovium, and peripheral blood mononuclear cells (six studies, 401,902 cells, 90 individuals) using Harmony. Pseudobulk differential expression and gene set enrichment analysis were performed at the tissue cell-compartment, cell-type, and subpopulation levels, including independent reclustering of lymphoid, myeloid and fibroblast populations. Results: Disease-associated transcriptional programmes showed marked tissue dependence, even within the same cell lineage, highlighting the importance of organ-specific mechanisms in SSc. Nevertheless, recurrent extracellular matrix (ECM) remodelling programmes were identified in lung, skin and synovium, and interferon signalling programmes in skin, synovium and peripheral blood mononuclear cells, across immune and fibroblast cell populations. Although no subpopulation was exclusive to SSc, a shared myofibroblast subpopulation expressing SFRP2, COL1A1, POSTN, ACTA2, and COMP was identified across lung, skin, and synovium. In addition, perivascular and mitotic fibroblast subpopulations exhibited both profibrotic and inflammatory signatures, including interferon- and IL-2-related signalling programmes. Conclusions: SSc is characterised by two complementary axes: a tissue-dependent cellular programme and a recurrent fibrotic and interferon-associated signature extending across multiple organs and cell populations. These findings are consistent with current organ-based therapeutic approaches while highlighting interferon signalling as a potential multi-organ therapeutic target. The resulting interactive single-cell atlas provides a resource for investigating shared and organ-specific disease mechanisms and guiding future therapeutic research.

Title: Lipopolysaccharide and Wzi retain capsular polysaccharide at the Klebsiella pneumoniae cell surface and promote bloodstream infection fitness
Authors: Khadka, S.; Resko, Z. J.; Shepard, G. E.; Kinney, E. L.; Gates, G. M.; Stark, D. J.; Mike, L. A.
Abstract: Bacterial capsules are formed by individual capsular polysaccharide (CPS) polymers and are the outermost extracellular layers of many Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. Capsules affect several aspects of bacterial biology, including resistance to host immune factors, survival in unfavorable environments and antimicrobial resistance. Research on CPS biology has largely focused on its synthesis and the pathogenic consequences of its presence or absence. Beyond synthesis, our understanding of its retention (attachment) on the cell surface is limited. Klebsiella pneumoniae is an important Gram-negative pathogen and expresses more than 80 capsular serotypes using the common Wzy-dependent CPS biosynthesis system and phenotypically manifests in various forms, making this species an attractive bacterial model to study the underexplored aspects of CPS biology. Here, we identified and characterized bacterial components involved in CPS retention in K. pneumoniae and assessed the importance of CPS retention on bloodstream fitness. Our examination revealed that lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and the outer-membrane protein, Wzi, collectively retain K. pneumoniae CPS on the bacterial surface. We demonstrate that the core-oligosaccharide domain of LPS and the extracellular surface of Wzi likely provide anchoring sites for CPS on the bacterial surface. Furthermore, CPS retention depends on divalent cation availability. Importantly, CPS retention on the bacterial surface is important for survival in serum and bacterial fitness at secondary infection sites in a murine bacteremia model. Together, our findings demonstrate that the functional importance of CPS to bacteria extends beyond synthesis and its overall abundance. Bacterial control over other CPS properties, like cell surface retention, are also important for K. pneumoniae fitness during bacteremia.

Title: The large conjugative plasmid pAB3 integrates into the chromosome of Acinetobacter baumannii ATCC 17978
Authors: Neil, M.; Langridge, G.; Evans, B. A.
Abstract: ATCC 17978 is one of the most utilised lab strains of Acinetobacter baumannii. Current literature suggests ATCC 17978 can have either a sulfamethoxazole-resistant phenotype or have the type VI secretion system (T6SS) switched on depending on the presence/absence of the large conjugative plasmid pAB3, which encodes the antimicrobial resistance gene (ARG) sul2 and T6SS repressors tetR1/tetR2. Here, we show that pAB3 integrates into the ATCC 17978 chromosome, which enables a large inversion resulting in the chromosomal arrangement labelled GS2.24 by Socru. This integration has no transcriptional impact on nearby genes or tetR1/tetR2. We find several instances were a portion of integrated pAB3 containing tetR2 is lost but the rest of the sequence, including sul2, is maintained, suggesting pAB3 integration may serve to make further rearrangements more tractable, enabling a putative T6SS+ sulfamethoxazole-resistant phenotype.

Title: YhdP forms an envelope-spanning phospholipid-binding bridge in complex with DedD
Authors: Tian, Q.; Clark, R.; Musto, I.; Kirschbaum, C.; Mitra, J.; Cooper, B. F.; Szczepaniak, J.; Bamber, M.; Robinson, C. V.; Khalid, S.; Isom, G.
Abstract: The outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria is built from phospholipids synthesised at the inner membrane, but how they cross the periplasm remains unresolved. YhdP is the leading candidate for anterograde phospholipid transfer and is predicted to form an envelope-spanning bridge. Here we purify YhdP at endogenous levels and show by cryo-electron microscopy that it contains a continuous cavity, alongside an additional density that proteomics identifies as the cell wall-binding protein DedD. Liposome co-sedimentation shows that the C-terminal helices of YhdP bind membranes directly, and single-molecule tracking reveals that endogenous YhdP is as immobile as an outer membrane protein, indicating an envelope-spanning architecture in vivo. Native mass spectrometry demonstrates that the YhdP groove accommodates all major classes of E. coli phospholipid without headgroup preference. DedD engages YhdP through its disordered region and increases lipid density at the groove entrance, suggesting a potential role in lipid loading.

Title: Metabolic cascades drive spatial prebiotic fermentation in a defined gut consortium
Authors: Berthold, D. L.; Realini, N. R.; Sichert, A.; Hausmann, A.; Sauer, U.
Abstract: Dietary fiber deficiency shifts the gut microbiota to degrade host mucus, compromising intestinal homeostasis. Mechanistically linking in vitro metabolic dynamics of fiber degradation to in vivo outcomes remains challenging due to a lack of representative model systems. Introducing spatial mucin structures to a defined Oligo-Mouse-Microbiota (OMM12) in vitro consortium allowed us to recapitulate the spatio-temporal dynamics of xylooligosaccharide (XOS) processing in gnotobiotic mice. XOS supplementation rapidly established a stable community state in vitro and in vivo across compositional, metabolic and transcriptional levels. XOS supplementation established distinct functional guilds: Bifidobacterium animalis and Blautia coccoides partitioning xylose and arabinose catabolism, whilst profiting from XOS degradation by Bacteroides caecimuris. Along the colonic axis, a spatial XOS gradient exposes Bl. coccoides's substrate preference for xylose and drives longitudinal functional adaptations. Altogether, our predictive platform proves that regional microenvironments govern prebiotic efficacy, highlighting spatial cascades as essential parameters for targeted microbiome interventions.

Title: Defective Viral Genomes Reveal History-dependent Self-regulation of Type I Interferon Dynamics
Authors: Li, Y.; Lourens, C.; Nielsen, B. F.; Levin, S.; Perelson, A. S.; Grenfell, B.; te Velthuis, A. J. W.
Abstract: Type I interferons (IFN) help clear a viral infection, but IFN levels can then decline to reset the antiviral state and avoid innate immune dysregulation. Such dysregulation can occur following infection with highly pathogenic and pandemic RNA viruses, such as H5N1 influenza A viruses or SARS-CoV-2. In spite of the strong innate immune response that these viruses induce, pandemic viruses replicate and spread successfully, suggesting that they can circumvent the effects of IFN. Innate immune activation is triggered when host cells detect viral RNA, especially defective viral genomes (DVGs). A strong IFN response (e.g. to DVGs or a highly immunogenic wild-type infection) must then decline through negative feedback involving the IFN receptor. How DVGs modulate this feedback remains poorly understood. To quantify positive and negative IFN regulation, we first performed in vitro experiments combining different doses of viral RNA and exogenous IFN, and measured subsequent IFN expression. We next developed an in vivo Bayesian computational model that captures the impact of influenza virus DVGs on both positive and negative IFN feedback. Competition between DVGs and virus is also considered. Finally, we calibrated this model on published in vitro and in vivo influenza virus infection data. Our model suggests that the cumulative IFN exposure of a host cell, rather than the instantaneous IFN level, shapes further IFN induction; this gives DVGs a dual role: beyond triggering IFN induction, they can also lower it through negative feedback. Our model further predicts that these effects are important locally, shaping the spatial dynamics of the response, allowing suppression of innate immune responses in neighbouring, uninfected cells. Through this model, we can explain two important biological observations: i) IFN levels can decline while virus and DVG levels continue to rise in tissue culture and mouse infections; and ii) pandemic viruses that produce high levels of immunogenic RNA molecules can successfully replicate through local innate immune suppression. Overall, we propose that heterogeneity within viral populations (including DVGs and other noncanonical viral RNAs) can modulate positive and negative feedback loops and shape infection outcomes. More broadly, our work may support studies into the therapeutic use of these viral RNA populations.

Title: Host identity drives distinct prokaryotic and microeukaryotic microbiomes across four cold-water coral species in a near-pristine Mediterranean reef.
Authors: Ardanaz Ullate, A.; Lo Iacono, C.; Agazzi, M.; del Campo, J.
Abstract: Cabliers is the widest Mediterranean cold-water coral (CWC) mound province exhibiting active growth. This area, a ridge-like CWC mound located in the Alboran Sea (SW Mediterranean) is characterized by thriving CWC reefs and accompanying mega-benthic communities (i.e.: gorgonians, black corals, sponges) found in near-pristine conditions and undergoing an almost null human pressure. We provide in this study the first characterization of the prokaryotic and microeukaryotic microbiomes of four key deep corals structuring the Cabliers province: Madrepora oculata, Desmophyllum pertusum, Leiopathes glaberrima, and Acanthogorgia hirsuta. We used DNA metabarcoding of the 16S and 18S rRNA gene V4 regions via Illumina MiSeq technology to elucidate symbiotic relationships that enable the holobiont to thrive. We found that host identity was the primary driver of microbial community structure, identifying specific signature microbiomes within coral species. The octocoral A. hirsuta showed reliance on microbes for organic matter processing such as the BD1-7 clade, while scleractinians M. oculata and D. pertusum displayed distinct symbionts, including Endozoicomonas (involved in the sulfur cycle) and the SUP05 clade, respectively. We suggest that coral microbiomes are vital for the continuous growth of Cabliers, with physiological needs and host identity shaping unique microbial communities within these deep coral ecosystems.

Title: Shared and Specific miRNA-mRNA in Human and Murine Acute Kidney Injury
Authors: Janosevic, D.; McCarthy, T. W.; Sadolikar, A.; Hato, T.; Eadon, M. T.; Dagher, P.; The Kidney Precision Medicine Project,
Abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is managed as a single clinical entity despite substantial biological heterogeneity. We established a cross-species framework to define etiology-specific molecular programs and determine how these programs relate to molecular heterogeneity and pathobiology in human AKI. We performed parallel sequencing of totalRNA (mRNA) and miRNA (kidney, whole blood) in 3 murine models (mild AKI: ischemia-reperfusion injury, IRI; cecal-ligation and puncture, CLP; endotoxemia, LPS); kidney mRNA and miRNA clearly distinguished the models, blood mRNA maintained model-specific separation, and blood miRNA was less distinct. IRI was characterized by epithelial injury/repair, and extracellular matrix remodeling (i.e., miR-125b-1-3p, Vim, Sprr2g); CLP, broader inflammatory, metabolic programs (i.e., miR-692, Pfkfb3, Cdo1); LPS, inflammatory signaling (i.e., miR-155-5p, Irf7, Gbp3). We then compared these signatures to human whole blood RNAseq. Human blood samples varied along a shared gene axis that correlated to differing degrees with all three murine models, consistent with the heterogeneous nature of clinical AKI rather than discrete assignment to a single experimental etiology. Orthologs were linked to immune processes (i.e., SIGLEC14, DAAM2, CD177, DEFA3), and the presence of tubular casts in human biopsies, reflecting that mild murine AKI models capture etiology-specific biology relevant to severe human AKI. Integration of injury etiology, severity, and time may provide a framework for developing circulating biomarkers that may resolve the biological heterogeneity of human AKI.

Title: SF3b inhibitors suppress proliferation of nonsmall cell lung cancer cells irrespective of EGFR mutation status
Authors: Fukagawa, W.; Horita, Y.; Harada, H.; Mori, M.; Murata, Y.; Ohe, K.
Abstract: Epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs) are standard care for EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but acquired resistance limits their durability, and alternatives that do not depend on EGFR kinase activity are needed. We asked whether inhibitors of SF3b, a core component of the U2 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein particle, act on NSCLC cells regardless of EGFR genotype. Three lung adenocarcinoma lines were treated with pladienolide B or herboxidiene at 0.01, 0.1 and 1 uM: PC9 and HCC827, both carrying an EGFR exon 19 deletion and both inhibited by gefitinib at nanomolar concentrations, and A549, which is EGFR wild type and gefitinibin sensitive. Proliferation was followed for three days by crystal violet staining, EGFR intron 2 retention was assayed by RTPCR, and EGFR protein was measured by western blotting. Both compounds produced a concentration-dependent increase in the intron 2 retained product in all three lines, and both held proliferation at or near the day 0 cell number in all three, at concentrations down to 0.01 uM. EGFR protein was lost in PC9, reduced in A549, and only partly reduced in HCC827, where a residual band persisted in lanes whose growth was fully suppressed. Since A549 is EGFR wild-type, and published knockdown data show that removing EGFR does not suppress proliferation of wild-type lines, the growth inhibition cannot be attributed to loss of EGFR alone. We read EGFR intron 2 retention as a marker of target engagement rather than as the mechanism of the growth effect. These are the results of single experiments without replicates or statistical testing and should be read as preliminary.

Title: Genomic Correlates of APOBEC-Associated Mutagenesis in Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma
Authors: Ansah, E. O.; Yentumi, J. A.; Kodom, E. Y.; Mensah, P. O.; Fosu, K.; Adu, I. K.; Boahen, E. A.
Abstract: Background and Aims: APOBEC-associated mutagenesis is prominent in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC), but genomic features associated with its intertumoral variability remain incompletely characterized. We investigated genomic correlates of APOBEC-associated mutagenesis while accounting for the compositional structure of mutational signature data. Methods: Mutational signatures were analyzed in 552 ESCC tumors from eight countries. APOBEC-associated mutagenesis was quantified as SBS2 plus SBS13 using absolute mutation counts and proportional contributions. Associations with co-occurring mutational signatures, total SBS burden, recurrent driver-gene alterations, and country were evaluated using correlation, sensitivity, and multivariable analyses. Principal component and regression-model robustness were additionally assessed. Results: APOBEC burden varied markedly across tumors (median, 2,002 mutations; IQR, 987-4,346). Several associations observed using signature proportions were not maintained in absolute-count analyses: SBS1, SBS3, and SBS5 changed direction, indicating sensitivity to compositional representation. In contrast, SBS18 remained inversely associated with APOBEC-associated mutagenesis in all variable pairings examined: proportion versus proportion (Spearman rho = -0.527), APOBEC proportion versus SBS18 absolute count (r = -0.435), and absolute count versus absolute count (Pearson r = -0.319, P = 1.59 x 10^-14; Spearman rho = -0.317). These are distinct comparisons rather than discrepant estimates. Notably, this cohort-wide relationship was primarily characterized by higher APOBEC burden in SBS18-negative than SBS18-positive tumors rather than a continuous inverse relationship among SBS18-positive tumors. The multivariable model had an in-sample R^2 of 0.400 but lower and variable 10-fold cross-validated performance (mean R^2 = 0.273). Country added little explanatory information to this model (delta R^2 = 0.008; global P = 0.402). ZNF750-mutant tumors had higher APOBEC burden than wild-type tumors (BH-FDR q = 0.0032), although only 12 tumors carried ZNF750 alterations. Conclusion: Genomic correlates of APOBEC-associated mutagenesis in ESCC are sensitive to the representation of mutational signature activity. SBS18 showed the most consistent inverse association, whereas the ZNF750 association warrants independent validation.

Title: Dissecting functional elements in giant genomes using the first generation of high quality salamander assemblies
Authors: Timoshevskaya, N.; Timoshevskiy, V. A.; Eskut, K. I.; Jarvis, E. D.; Voss, S. R.; Smith, J. J.
Abstract: Salamanders are an enduring and historically significant group that helped originate multiple scientific fields of study, including regeneration, cytogenetics, experimental embryology, cloning, evolutionary developmental biology and evolution of extreme genome size. We generated a high-quality, single haplotype assembly for the 32 Gb axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum) genome using an F1 hybrid between axolotl and a divergent relative the tiger salamander (A. tigrinum). Using multi-genome alignments to other salamanders that meet VGP metrics, we leveraged strong conservation of karyotypic structure to identify >523,000 highly conserved non-coding elements within massively expanded intronic and intergenic regions, the vast majority of which are unique to the salamander lineage. Orthogonal measures of chromatin state and enhancer activity confirmed that many conserved elements correspond to cis-regulatory sequences and identified several thousand that are utilized during regeneration. The conserved elements identified here will enable robust functional genomic analyses of tissue regeneration and other traits that uniquely empower salamander models in biological research.

Title: Impaired loading following denervation elicits dynamic, differential growth trajectories of musculoskeletal tissues
Authors: Johnson, T.; Fogarty, N.; Hallstrom, G.; Miller, D.; Dennis, M.; Lin, A.; Jiang, X.; Xiang, J.; Boerckel, J. D.; Koyama, E.; Han, L.; Baxter, J. R.; Mauck, R.; Dyment, N.
Abstract: Physical forces dictate the function and maintenance of adult musculoskeletal tissues. Yet, the impact of biophysical cues on the growth and maturation of these tissues, especially dense connective tissues, remains unclear. Here, we investigated the effects of neonatal mechanical loading on early postnatal growth of the musculoskeletal tissues of the lower limb, with particular focus on the Achilles tendon. We performed sciatic nerve resection (SNR) on one-day-old mice to denervate the hamstrings and distal hindlimb muscles. Sciatic Nerve Resection resulted in severe and sustained alterations in gait, accompanied by an altered transcriptional landscape in distal musculoskeletal tissues, with marked reductions in bone and tendon growth and smaller, fibrotic hindlimb musculature. Sciatic nerve resection impaired cumulative growth in the Achilles tendon, shifting cell proliferation and matrix-driven growth trajectories and altering mechanotransduction gene programs toward inflammation and matrix catabolism with age. This work highlights the essential role of mechanical loading in driving mechanosignaling and postnatal growth trajectories in musculoskeletal tissues of the developing limb, with implications for overall musculoskeletal health in adulthood.

Title: Structure-resolved fold annotation of the medicinal-leech salivary-EV cargo: a Ly-6/uPAR three-finger scaffold and a structurally dark fraction
Authors: Cen, H.; Zhao, F.; Zhao, J.; Tong, X.; Liu, Z.; Zhao, F.
Abstract: Many proteins that medicinal leeches package into salivary extracellular vesicles (EVs) carry no interpretable sequence annotation, so the least-characterised part of a pharmacologically important secretome lacks even a fold assignment. A companion Astral-DIA study of Hirudinaria manillensis nominated 17 ultra-enriched candidate EV cargo proteins. Here we ask whether structure prediction and structural search can assign folds where sequence methods fail, and which candidates remain unresolved under prespecified criteria. With an offline pipeline (ESMFold, TM-align, Foldseek against AFDB-SwissProt and PDB100, UniRef90 search, protein-to-genome alignment), the candidates separate into intracellular/membrane machinery and a secreted, cysteine-dense fraction of three proteins with no Pfam domain. The predicted structure of the leech Protein-sleepless homolog g21166 supports its assignment to the Ly-6/uPAR three-finger fold (TM 0.58 vs CD59; best significant PDB match Lynx1); no function is inferred. g436 and g20791 returned no match meeting the criterion (alnTM [≥] 0.5, E [≤] 0.05) in either database, g436 even after homolog-informed modelling. Gene structure and splice junctions support a conserved locus for the two-Trypsin-segment model g8114 (catalytic unit not established). A Boltz-2 thrombin pilot did not support target engagement, and a pre-registered nicotinic test was terminated as undecidable. The results yield a structure-informed shortlist for experimental follow-up.

Title: Laminin-Derived Peptides Bind Neuropilin-1 at the VEGF-A165 Binding Pocket
Authors: Veltri, E.; Lovas, S.
Abstract: Neuropilin-1 (NRP-1) is associated with glioblastoma progression and contains a b1-domain pocket that binds the C-terminal region of VEGF-A165. Whether laminin-derived peptide fragments can associate with this site is unknown. AlphaFold 3 complex prediction followed by 15 s of all-atom production molecular dynamics simulation, trajectory-based pocket occupancy and interaction analyses, and FoldX energetic scoring was performed to compare binding of the laminin-derived pentapeptide Ac-Tyr-Ile-Gly-Ser-Arg-NH2 (peptide 1) with its retro (Ac-Arg-Ser-Gly-Ile-Tyr-NH2, peptide 2) and retro-inverso (Ac-arg-ser-Gly-ile-tyr-NH2, peptide 3) analogs. Peptide 1 showed the highest mean equilibrated occupancy of the canonical VEGF-A165 pocket (60.3 +/- 34.6%) compared with peptide 2 (25.9 +/- 32.7%) and peptide 3 (21.4 +/- 29.5%), while sampling interactions with canonical pocket residues including Asp320, Tyr297, and Tyr353; FoldX binding-energy estimates were similar across peptides despite their differing pocket persistence. Complementary nanoDSF measurements using recombinant NRP-1 and synthetic peptides yielded apparent dissociation constants in the low micromolar range for all three peptides (12.7 M - 33.3 M), providing experimental support for the predicted interactions. These results support persistent, sequence-dependent association of peptide 1 with the VEGF-A165 binding site of b1-NRP-1 and identify peptide analogs as a candidate for further optimization as an NRP-1-binding peptide.

Title: Mathematical Modeling of AA Amyloidosis: Coupling SAA-HDL Binding Dynamics with Path-Dependent Renal Aging
Authors: Kuznetsov, A. V.
Abstract: Why does chronic inflammation cause AA amyloidosis in only some patients, even when serum amyloid A (SAA) remains elevated in many? This study proposes that disease progression is governed by two linked nonlinear processes: saturation of the finite SAA-binding capacity of high-density lipoprotein (HDL), followed by autocatalytic aggregation of amyloid A (AA) in the kidney. A hypothesis-generating mathematical model is developed that couples reversible SAA-HDL binding to renal filtration of free SAA, lysosomal cleavage to AA fragments, Finke-Watzky aggregation, oligomer deposition, and fibril turnover. As total SAA rises beyond the effective HDL binding capacity, the model predicts a disproportionate increase in free, filterable SAA available for renal amyloid formation. A dimensionless reduction reveals two kinetic regimes separated by a threshold at which autocatalytic oligomer production balances oligomer loss. Below this threshold, aggregation is nucleation-limited; above it, the system becomes supply-limited and is controlled mainly by upstream SAA delivery. In the zero-primary-nucleation limit, the two steady-state branches exchange stability at this threshold, giving a transcritical bifurcation that finite primary nucleation smooths into a continuous transition. The baseline parameter set lies in the supply-limited regime, explaining why total SAA concentration and effective HDL binding-site capacity have the largest local sensitivities, with SAA-HDL affinity and lysosomal cleavage next in rank, whereas the aggregation rate constants have small local effects but can still determine which regime applies. The model further predicts that the temporal pattern of inflammation matters: intermittent SAA flares can produce several-fold more renal damage than sustained inflammation with the same mean SAA, and earlier SAA suppression leaves a lower renal biological-age index, a calibrated measure of cumulative damage, than later suppression. Published SAA-outcome data are consistent with the predicted SAA dependence. By linking HDL buffering to renal SAA delivery, nonlinear aggregation, and cumulative injury, the model provides a quantitative framework for identifying amyloidogenic transitions and testing how SAA control can alter renal disease progression.

Title: A collaborative submission model for building high-quality data resources at scale through partnership: lessons from single-cell genomics
Authors: Hilton, J. A.; Chaffer, J.; Chien, J.; Gabdank, I.; Mott, B.; Rutherford, E.; Small, C.; Zamanian, J.; Aevermann, B.; Cherry, J. M.; Klein, T. E.
Abstract: Community data resources that aggregate datasets across studies are critical infrastructure for modern biomedical research, accelerating discovery, and rapidly-advancing Artificial Intelligence (AI) models place ever-greater demand on large, well-described data corpora. However, building these resources involves a fundamental tension: comprehensive metadata is imperative for reuse, yet capturing this information systematically requires substantial effort that limits growth. We detail how CZ CELLxGENE Discover has used a collaborative submission model, whereby data contributors partner with dedicated resource curators, to become a large, widely used single-cell genomics resource for diverse analytical applications including AI model development and integrative analysis. This partnership leverages contributors' intimate study knowledge and curators' focus on data reuse and expertise in standardization to improve data quality, metadata accuracy, and richness. This is achieved by motivating researcher participation through tangible benefits while minimizing submission burden. We contrast this collaborative model with contributor-driven and resource-driven approaches, highlighting tradeoffs in scalability, consistency across submissions, and quality assurance. The principles and practices we describe provide a framework for building high-quality community data resources across diverse biological data types.

Title: An agent-built, verified atlas of public spatial transcriptomics shows that breadth across studies drives transfer and reproducibility
Authors: Ji, J.-H.; Zou, Q.; Cheng, J.; She, Z.; Hao, Y.; Liu, W.; Zhang, D.; Wang, Z.; Yu, J.-T.; Yuan, Z.
Abstract: Public spatial transcriptomics data are deposited study by study, in formats that differ from one laboratory to the next, and no resource has yet indexed or verified them as a whole. Here we present SpatialDataAgent-DB, an atlas built from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) by SpatialDataAgent, a workflow in which language-model agents do the work and every output is checked rather than trusted. An assay index covering all 298,179 GEO series identifies 2,411 spatial series, which gives public spatial data an explicit denominator. For each series, an agent writes conversion code instead of editing the data directly, and a frozen, rule-based scorer recomputes every released value from the source files. In a held-out test, the scorer rejected all 1,231 corrupted copies. We also visually reviewed every released sample, including the 4,386 H&E-registered Visium samples of our earlier HESRT release. SpatialDataAgent-DB contains 12,163 samples from 12 platforms and 42 species in a single format, each with its provenance and defect flags. Its 8,211 image-paired samples are 5.9 times as many as in the next image-paired resource, and at least 71% of all samples are absent from five existing catalogues. Without batch correction, sequencing-based samples group by organ more than by platform: with platforms balanced, organ explains 32% of the variance of human pseudobulk profiles and platform 13% (mouse, 47% and 18%). We then used the atlas in two applications. Image-to-expression models trained on it transfer to unseen studies, and their accuracy rises steadily with training data and, at a fixed number of patches, with the number of training studies over the range tested (for H&E, Pearson r gains 0.0056 per doubling of training patches up to 524,288); 11 of 13 forecasts locked in advance were confirmed. Adding studies helps more than adding patches from the same studies, because each study leaves a fingerprint in its images. Intent-based search over the same index assembled 70 single-cell dementia studies, and the replication of disease signatures in held-out studies rose steadily with the number of studies (direction agreement averaged over 28 held-out studies, 63% with one study and 77% with 16). In both applications, performance kept rising with the number of independent studies, which a complete and verified atlas is built to provide.

Title: Microbead-Based Heterodimer Assay for Amplification-Free Detection of Single-Stranded DNA
Authors: Roy, S. R.; Lobato-Dauzier, N.; Mateos, J.; Tauran, Y.; Brioude, A.; Baccouche, A.; Fujii, T.; Genot, A. J.; Kim, S. H.
Abstract: Direct detection of rare nucleic-acid targets without molecular amplification requires specific recognition events to be made observable while remaining distinguishable from nonspecific interactions. Here, we introduce a microbead-based heterodimer assay (MBHA) that converts two-site recognition of single-stranded DNA into spatially resolved, two-color bead-pairing events for direct nucleic-acid detection. Two spectrally distinct microbead populations are functionalized with partially double-stranded DNA probes exposing target-binding domains complementary to separate regions of the target. Target-mediated bridging produces heterotypic bead pairs that are classified by fluorescence identity and an interparticle-distance criterion, while residual background is evaluated relative to blank measurements. Under the tested conditions, 166 fM was the lowest target concentration exceeding the blank-derived detection threshold. A sequence-scrambled synthetic non-target DNA remained below threshold across the tested concentration range, and detection at 166 fM was retained in the presence of 1 uM non-target DNA, corresponding to an approximately six-million-fold molar excess. Probe redesign further extended the assay to a second 60-nucleotide synthetic DNA target derived from the SARS-CoV-2 ORF1ab sequence. This proof-of-concept study establishes heterodimer counting as an amplification-free measurement strategy in which rare molecular-recognition events are made directly observable and individually classifiable without increasing target copy number.

Title: Temporal Phosphoproteomic Network Reconstruction of Condition-Dependent EGFR Signaling Routes Through Unmeasured Proteins
Authors: Lee, H.; Lee, G.
Abstract: Time-resolved phosphoproteomics captures fast signaling dynamics, but proteins that show no phosphorylation change, or escape detection, leave gaps the data cannot bridge. TS-BFS-BS uses the temporal order of a phosphoproteomic time course to guide a beam-pruned breadth-first search over STRING v12.5 functional, physical, and regulatory priors, returning temporally continuous routes that can pass through unmeasured bridge proteins. In EGF time courses from MDA-MB-468, EGFR Flp-In HEK293T and HeLa cells, endpoints and short routes were stable across search settings, and endpoints were largely shared across STRING priors, whereas long routes depended on settings and prior. When measured hubs CBL and SRC were removed, both were recovered as bridges and 94-99% of endpoints were retained. Incorrect temporal orders gave endpoint Jaccard indices of only 0.23-0.33 with the correct order, comparable to SHP2 inhibition (0.25-0.35), under which PTPN11 was excluded from all routes by its measured pretreatment response and returned after washout. TS-BFS-BS generates time-resolved, testable signaling hypotheses for iterative refinement.

Title: Assessment of Q-PCR based vector copy numbers and viral titration in CAR T cell products, Probe vs SYBR Green.
Authors: Ebrahimiyan, H.; Sayadmanesh, A.; Moradmand, A.; Basiri, M.; Baharvand, H.
Abstract: Assessment of vector copy numbers (VCNs) in comprised of the chimeric antigen receptor (CAR (T cells as a safety parameter and viral titration in the vector bank (VB) as an efficacy parameter are essential in the CAR T cell production procedure. Here, we developed a quantitative-PCR (Q-PCR) based VCN and viral titration analysis using both Probe and SYBR Green methods. Cellular viral titration was also applied for comparison of viral titration results. The VCN in CAR T cells with SYBR Green was 1.72, 2.31, and 2.46 respectively, while in the Probe based analysis, it was 1.33, 1.83, and 2.20. The molecular viral titration in SYBR Green resulted in 2.90*109, 5.24*1010, and 9.76*1010, while in the Probe it was 1.54*109, 1.13*109, and 7.73*108. The cellular titration resulted in 1.73*106, 2.16*106, and 2.49*106. In summary, both SYBR Green and Probe revealing that Probe strategy had a lower dependency on sample contamination and could be a better strategy for the Q-PCR method. The SYBR Green based viral titration method is significantly different from the Probe based method, with the Probe based method yielding better results compared to the cellular titration method. However, no significant difference was reported in both methods for VCNs.

Title: Engineered trophoblast organoids recapitulate molecular and functional features of preeclampsia
Authors: Arthurs, A. L.; Lushington, C.; Medina Garcia, D. L.; Merriman, A. L.; Mora-Roldan, G. A.; Parry, L.; Boparai, A.; Polo, J. M.; Adikusuma, F. L.; Thomas, P. Q.; Roberts, C. T.
Abstract: Preeclampsia is a major pregnancy complication driven by placental dysfunction, yet research is limited by reliance on patient-derived tissues and models that do not fully capture human disease. Here, we develop a genetically engineered human trophoblast organoid model of preeclampsia that can be generated without access to placental tissue. Using a CRISPR-based Prime Integrase strategy, we engineered induced trophoblast stem cells to express the preeclampsia-associated soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1) exon 15a isoform. Engineered organoids showed a transcriptional shift towards primary preeclamptic placentae and developed several features of disease. These included reduced PlGF, increased IL-6 and soluble endoglin, oxidative stress, impaired growth and an elevated sFlt-1/PlGF ratio comparable to primary preeclamptic trophoblast organoids. These broader changes were not reproduced by adding recombinant human sFlt-1 to control organoids. Conditioned media from engineered organoids impaired endothelial network formation, demonstrating a functional effect of the altered trophoblast secretome. Treatment with sulfasalazine and metformin also restored angiogenic balance and organoid growth. Together, these findings establish a tractable human model that reproduces molecular and functional features of preeclampsia and provides a platform to study disease mechanisms and test potential therapies.

Title: Germline stem cell isolation, lineage tracing, and aging in a protochordate
Authors: Levy, T.; Anselmi, C.; Ishizuka, K. J.; Gordon, T.; Voskoboynik, Y.; McGeever, E.; Detweiler, A. M.; Levin, L.; Palmeri, K. J.; Liu, D. D.; Sinha, R.; Ohene-Gambill, B. F.; Raveh, T.; Morri, M.; Vanni, V.; Manni, L.; Sahoo, D.; Neff, N. F.; Rosental, B.; Weissman, I. L.; Voskoboynik, A.
Abstract: Germline stem cells (GSCs), the source of gametes, are the only stem cells capable of passing genes to future generations making them cellular units of natural selection. Yet, factors regulating their fitness, and thus governing GSC competition, which exist in both protochordates and mammals, remain poorly understood. We study how aging affects GSC fitness in the protochordate Botryllus schlosseri, an evolutionary crosspoint between invertebrates and vertebrates. GSCs were isolated using flow cytometry and characterized by single-cell RNA sequencing, supported by a new PacBio genome assembly. GSC transplantation assays confirmed their function, further validated through a transgenerational lineage tracing strategy combining membrane-labeling dyes and single-cell transcriptomic analysis. Leveraging our method to isolate them, we uncover significant age-related changes in GSCs, while spermatids and sperm show minimal differences, suggesting that reproductive aging is influenced primarily by GSCs rather than by gametes. Reduced expression of markers like DDX4 and PIWIL1 in aged GSCs mirrors trends in mammalian datasets, suggesting conserved age-associated molecular changes in GSCs across chordate evolution. This study provides new techniques that lay the foundation to investigate further drivers of GSC fitness and highlights fertility-related genes as promising targets for therapies to preserve reproductive health.

Title: The effect of a reduction in population size on mean fitness and inbreeding depression
Authors: Lopez-Cortegano, E.; Charlesworth, B.
Abstract: A sudden reduction in population size increases the rate of genetic drift, reducing variability and increasing the mean level of homozygosity. The resulting increase in exposure of strongly deleterious, recessive or partially recessive alleles to selection against homozygotes may lead to their being purged from the population, potentially allowing mean fitness to increase after an initial decline, and accelerating the decline in inbreeding depression associated with reduced variability. However, detailed population genetic theory on the effects of population bottlenecks on mean fitness and inbreeding depression remains limited. We develop a theoretical framework for small, randomly mating populations founded from a large population at mutation-selection-drift equilibrium, using both simulations and approximate analytical results. These provide quantitative predictions for the dynamics of the population's mean fitness and level of inbreeding depression following a bottleneck. In particular, we derive an approximate expression for the time needed for mean fitness to recover after an initial decline; such a recovery requires selection to be sufficiently strong relative to drift, and mutations to be sufficiently recessive. In contrast, weakly deleterious mutations cause reductions in mean fitness and inbreeding depression that are similar in size to those predicted from increases in homozygosity for neutral alleles, over the relatively short timescales considered here.

Title: Single-nucleus profiling reveals age-associated remodeling opposed by parity in the postmenopausal human ovary
Authors: Byrne, J.; Martin, N.; Watson, M. A.; Soygur, B.; Devrukhkar, P. R.; Tran, T.; Shanes, E.; Pavone, M. G.; Duncan, F.; Schilling, B.
Abstract: The postmenopausal ovary is commonly viewed as a largely quiescent organ, yet its cellular biology remains incompletely characterized. We generated a single-nucleus atlas of the aging postmenopausal human ovary comprising 439,011 nuclei across 64 ovarian samples from 28 donors. We resolved 37 cell states, revealing extensive stromal, vascular, and immune heterogeneity. We developed an interactive data explorer to facilitate interrogation of cell annotations and gene expression across the atlas. Aging was associated with expansion of stress-associated stromal states, vascular and immune depletion, and a shift toward steroidogenic and androgen-responsive programs. Several major age-associated compositional shifts were supported in an external GTEx ovary bulk RNA-seq cohort, validating relevance. Parity (1-3 versus 0 live births) was associated with transcriptional and compositional patterns broadly opposing age-associated remodeling. Our findings establish the postmenopausal ovary as an actively remodeled aging tissue and link obstetric history to molecular and cellular signatures detectable later in life.

Title: Transcript quantification using context-aware MAPQ modeling
Authors: Parthiban, S.; Hicks, S. C.
Abstract: Long-read RNA-sequencing enables accurate transcript-level quantification, but prior static filtering of MAPping Quality (MAPQ) can ignore transcriptome-intrinsic ambiguity, and discarding reads on this basis distorts abundance estimates. We present CALMeR (Context-Aware Long-read MAPQ-based Rescuer), which conditions MAPQ filtering on transcript properties rather than a fixed cutoff. CALMeR fits a zero-one inflated beta regression on various transcript and read-level features to model the expected MAPQ distribution for each alignment. Reads whose MAPQ fits this context, such as low-MAPQ reads from multi-isoform genes and paralog families are retained; reads with anomalously low MAPQ are removed as likely artifacts. Retained reads can be summed per transcript or passed to any downstream quantifier. Compared with a MAPQ [≥] 1 filter and expectation-maximization-based transcript quantification methods, CALMeR recovers more spike-in transcripts and better matches known spike-in concentrations. CALMeR is available at https://github.com/sparthib/CALMeR.

Title: BlastPhyMe: A toolkit for rapid generation and analysis of protein-coding sequence datasets
Authors: Gow, D.; Ballesteros, A.; Chang, B. S.; Schott, R. K.
Abstract: SUMMARY: We present BlastPhyMe (BLAST, Phylogenies, and Molecular Evolution) a new application to facilitate the fast and easy generation and analysis of protein-coding sequence datasets. The application uses a portable database framework to manage and organize sequences along with a graphical user interface (GUI) that makes the application extremely easy to use. BlastPhyMe utilizes several existing services and applications in a unique way that save researchers considerable time when building and analyzing protein-coding datasets. The application consists of two modules that can be used separately or together. The first module enables the assembly of coding sequence datasets. BLAST searches can be used to obtain all related sequences of interest from NCBI. Full GenBank records are saved within the database and coding sequences are automatically extracted. A feature of particular note is that sequences can be sorted based on NCBI taxonomic hierarchy before export for visualization using existing tools, such as fast. The application provides GUIs for automatic alignment of sequences with the popular tools MUSCLE and PRANK, as well as for reconstructing phylogenetic trees using PhyML. The second module incorporates selection analyses using codon-based likelihood methods. The alignments and phylogenetic trees generated with the dataset module, or those generated elsewhere, can be used to run the models implemented in the codeml PAML package. A GUI allows easy selection of models and parameters. Importantly, replicate analyses with different parameter starting values can be automatically performed in order to ensure selection of the best-fitting model. Multiple analyses can be run simultaneously based on the number of processor cores available, while additional analyses will be run iteratively until completed. Results are saved within the database and can be exported to publication-ready Excel tables, which further automatically compute the appropriate likelihood ratio test between models in order to determine statistical significance. Future updates will add additional options for phylogenetic reconstruction (eg, MrBayes) and selection analyses (eg, HYPHY). BlastPhyMe saves researches of all bioinformatics experience levels considerable time by automating the numerous tasks required for the generation and analysis of protein-coding sequence datasets using a straightforward graphical interface. AVAILABILITY: Installation package and source code available from: https://github.com/ryankschott/BlastPhyMe

Title: Structure constrained spin responses of an FMN superoxide radical-pair model in mitochondrial complex I
Authors: Sung, J.-Y.; Antill, L. M.; Cheong, J.-H.
Abstract: Mitochondrial complex I produces reactive oxygen species at its flavin mononucleotide (FMN) cofactor. We combined steric sampling of oxygen positions in human complex I with radical-pair spin simulations to examine how the FMN pocket shapes reaction yield sensitivity, which provided singlet yields across FMN O2 centroid separations, magnetic fields and spin dephasing conditions. When candidate oxygen positions overlapping the FMN cofactor itself were excluded, almost no accessible positions remained within 3.3 A of the isoalloxazine centre (0.2%), and a composite score combining geometric accessibility with normalised field and dephasing responses had no near-contact maximum. In the reference structure (PDB 5XTD), the highest-scoring 10% of accessible configurations had a mean separation of 5.8 A (2.5th~97.5th percentiles, 5.6~6.0 A); in the independently determined 9TI4 structure, the corresponding mean was 7.9 A (7.7~8.0 A), reflecting differences in the modelled pocket. Within each structure, this location changed little when the dephasing model, flavin hyperfine parameters, steric radii and recombination/dephasing rates were varied. Over 2.5~20 A, the exchange only score formed a broad plateau without a localized maximum. Small prescribed fluctuations in separation produced less singlet yield variability in the high scoring configurations than elsewhere in the accessible ensemble. A near contact score maximum reported in an earlier version of this analysis arose because positions overlapping FMN had been counted as accessible. The accessibility-weighted spin-response map of the complex I flavin site is therefore set mainly by pocket geometry and should be evaluated over structural ensembles rather than a single model.
